articles.title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky – this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
articles.author: David Hu, Professor of Mechanical Engineering and Biology, Adjunct Professor of Physics, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: Here’s a bit of a riddle for you: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects?

The medical term for earwax is cerumen, based on keros, the Greek word for beeswax. People have been pondering earwax since ancient times. Ancient hygiene kits including picks and spoons to remove earwax have been found in archaeological sites worldwide.

Even today, it remains a perpetual question: to remove or not to remove your earwax? The answer: Don’t do it. The general medical belief is that ears are self-cleaning, and earwax brings benefits such as lubricating the ear canal, fighting infection and acting like a sticky net to trap debris before it reaches the eardrum. By poking in there you can accidentally make matters worse, pushing wax deeper or scratching your delicate ear canal.

Cerumen impaction – or blocked earwax – affects about a fifth of the American population, leading to 12 million patient visits per year. Blockages are worsened by daily activities such as wearing earbuds or hearing aids.

Another common problem with ears is wedged debris. For children, much of this is self-inflicted, in the form of items such as Legos or erasers. But for many adults who have something stuck in their ear, the debris is insects, such as ants, beetles, flies or cockroaches.

While rare for the average person, insects in the ear occurred with such frequency over the years that physicians began to wonder whether earwax evolved as a natural barrier for insects. But how would such a barrier work?

To answer this question, my Ph.D. student David Ancalle led experiments with earwax and insects. We teamed up with Yuhang Hu and her student Donjing He, experts in the behavior of soft solids such as hydrogels. As mechanical engineers, we wanted to focus on the physics rather than the chemistry of earwax.
Our research, published in the journal Soft Matter, shows that earwax can, in fact, stop insects without the use of dangerous chemicals.
Watching ants encounter earwax
To do experiments, we needed voluminous amounts of earwax.

Initially we obtained earwax from deceased mammals such as pigs, sheep and rabbits. Eventually we turned to our friends and family. A person has only a grain of rice’s worth of earwax in each ear. Due to a mutation in a single gene, East Asians have dry, flaky earwax, while people of African or European descent have wet, squishy earwax.

To simulate an ant climbing into an ear canal, we used a glass beaker with its rim coated in earwax. Ants, like many insects, are climbing specialists, capable of traveling across many kinds of surfaces. To climb rough surfaces, ants have spikes on their feet, like mountain climbers do, that helps them grasp onto ridges and cracks. For smooth surfaces, ants unfurl wet suction cups, which can support 60 times their body weight on smooth glass.
Watching ants trying to climb earwax showed us how strange a substance it really is. Rough earwax slowed them down, but with their claws they made progress.
But as soon as ants tried to climb smooth earwax, they fell immediately.
From these experiments, we concluded that earwax had anti-stick properties when in contact with the insects’ feet.

We next conducted experiments with ants crawling through an earwax-coated tunnel, more similar in size to a human ear canal. As the ants attempted to travel through the tunnel, earwax stuck to them. Once coated, they groomed furiously, unwilling to walk until they had removed as much as possible. Even after several minutes of effort, the ants still had earwax sticking to hard-to-reach places.

So, earwax is a paradoxical material: It is simultaneously slippery, thanks to the lipids it contains, but also sticky. Similar to many materials – including ketchup, paint and shampoo – it thins out when it is physically deformed, what physicists call shear-thinning.
Figuring out earwax’s physical properties

The dual qualities of earwax have to do with its unique composition. Earwax is made up of flakes of skin cells held together with a binder. This blend forms a kind of sponge with microscopic holes. When a body overproduces earwax, it heaps up in boulders that ants can easily climb over.

When the substance is smooth, however, ants rely on their wet suction cups. The holes in the earwax absorb the drops produced by the ants, preventing them from attaching. Absorbency makes earwax fundamentally different from commonly used forms of pest control.

In your local store, you will find sticky surfaces such as fly paper or chemicals that kill the insects. Some researchers look to nature to find bio-friendly alternatives to using chemicals; for example, plants have properties that prevent insects from climbing.
From this study, we learned that the ear is also a model for insect repellency. Earwax is made of natural materials but has a structure that prevents ants from sticking to it.

The porosity of earwax also gives it unique properties. We showed it can absorb twice its weight in water yet still cling to the walls of the ear. This water-absorbing ability may help prevent water from accumulating on the delicate eardrum and fend off infections such as swimmer’s ear.
Scientists don’t yet understand the complex relationship between earwax, water and bacteria. Some studies show that earwax kills bacteria, but other studies find that earwax harbors bacteria.

Our experiments showed that earwax is most challenging to insects when similar to the thin layer of earwax maintained by a healthy human body. Wax would accumulate more in human ears if not for two self-cleaning mechanisms. The skin in the ear canal grows outward like a conveyor belt. Over 8-10 weeks, this process – called epithelial migration – pushes the oldest earwax out of the ear.

Simultaneously, earwax dries over time, transforming from a gooey state to a brittle one that readily cracks. Every time you talk or chew, your ear canal deforms, and physicians found that this movement helps to dislodge the drier, older earwax.

As a test of our concept, a member of our team, chemical engineer Rafeen Rahaman, designed an artificial earwax based on the physical structure rather than the chemistry of the earwax. Ants struggled when they touched it, just like when they interacted with natural earwax.

The cost of harvesting natural earwax and our recipe for artificial earwax are not cheap. We don’t foresee our methods replacing insect repellents produced at large scale. But perhaps the concept might inspire new ways to prevent earwax from coating our earbuds or lead to the manufacture of insect control methods using safe formulations.

articles.title: We studied 1,584 data centers – and found the buildings full of machines are tied to modest local job growth
articles.author: Simon Buechler, Assistant Professor of Finance, Miami University
paras: Data centers require enormous investments: land, buildings, computer equipment and power infrastructure. Yet, once they’re up and running, they tend to employ no more than a few dozen people in occupations such as IT technicians, engineers and security guards. With billions of dollars flowing into new data centers across the United States, communities are asking what they will get in return.

Skepticism about the local benefits of data centers is contributing to growing opposition to their construction, from Ohio to Texas. That pushback contributed to delays or cancellations of US$156 billion in proposed data center projects in 2025 alone.

We are professors who study real estate and urban economics, including how large place-based investments shape local economies. So we set out to answer a question at the center of these fights: Do data centers actually create jobs where they are built?

To find out, we teamed up with four colleagues to study what happens to local employment after data centers open. We found that new data centers that opened from 2000-2023 created 1,000 to 1,300 jobs in the counties where they are located, on average. But those jobs, which are for work performed outside data centers rather than inside them, take a few years to appear. They are mostly in industries that support data centers, not in restaurants or shops.
How data centers create local jobs
Data centers can create jobs in at least three ways beyond employing people who work inside them.
First, they can increase demand for local suppliers, from security companies that protect the facilities to electrical contractors that maintain their equipment.
Second, data center employees and workers at these suppliers may spend more money locally, supporting restaurants, stores and other local services.

Third, companies already operating data centers may expand their facilities, while other operators may decide to build nearby. Once a location has the electricity, fiber connections and other infrastructure needed to operate a data center, further investment may become easier.
Tracking data centers and jobs

We assembled detailed information on 1,584 U.S. data centers that opened between 2000 and 2023. For each facility, we recorded its location, opening date and power capacity, which is a standard way to compare facilities of different sizes. We then matched these records with federal data on employment, wages and the number of businesses in each county.

Isolating the effect of data centers isn’t straightforward. Operators don’t choose locations randomly. They look for reliable electricity, fiber connections, available land and friendly local regulations. Those places may already be growing, so new jobs might have appeared even without a data center.

To account for this, we tracked employment in counties that received data centers – such as Loudoun County in Virginia, Berkeley County in South Carolina, Morrow County in Oregon, and others – before and after the operation of the facility began. We then compared those trends with similar counties that did not receive data centers. We also looked at whether larger facilities brought bigger job gains.
Jobs appear, but not immediately

During the first two years after a county’s first data center opened, we found little change in employment outside construction. After that, jobs begin to grow. Three to five years after a center opened, we found that these counties had roughly 1,000 to 1,300 additional nonconstruction jobs than comparable counties without data centers.
Bigger investments brought bigger employment gains. Five years after new data center capacity is installed, each additional megawatt is associated with about 7.4 more nonconstruction local jobs.

Part of that gain, however, reflects further expansion. Each megawatt installed is associated with another 1.7 megawatts of capacity over the following years. Once that later growth is counted, our estimates work out to about 2.7 nonconstruction jobs per megawatt of eventual data center capacity. A large 100-megawatt facility, for example, would be correlated with roughly 275 additional local jobs outside the data center itself.
Jobs are not where you might expect
The types of jobs created help explain what is happening.

Employment gains are concentrated in transportation and warehousing, professional and technical services and real estate. These industries may serve or benefit directly from data centers or from the investment and infrastructure they bring.
By contrast, we found little evidence of job growth in restaurants, stores and other local services.

We also found that more data center investment tends to follow in the same county. Most often, the companies already operating in a county expand their facilities. Other companies generally don’t move into that same area to build new data centers.
Jobs are only one side of the equation

Our study has limits. It covers data centers that opened through 2023, before the current wave of massive facilities were built to power AI. Larger data centers do not necessarily create proportionally more jobs, so our findings may not apply to today’s biggest projects.

We also looked only at job gains and did not explore whether data centers are worth their cost to local communities. These facilities consume large amounts of electricity and water, can generate noise and may receive substantial tax breaks from local and state governments. We did not address any of those concerns.

Our findings do show that data centers can create jobs beyond the small number of people working inside their walls. But that does not mean every one of them is a good deal for their local community. And whether those additional jobs justify the costs remains an open question.

articles.title: How should AI be regulated? Follow the harm
articles.author: Sylvia Lu, Assistant Professor of Law, American University
paras: As artificial intelligence technologies grow ever more powerful, so do the risks they pose and with them the urgency of regulating AI.

In July 2026, OpenAI’s advanced models hacked into AI company Hugging Face’s systems during internal cybersecurity evaluations by communicating through unauthorized channels and working around safeguards developers had imposed on the models. In January 2026, Google and Character.ai, which makes a role-playing AI chatbot, agreed to settle a wrongful death lawsuit brought by Megan Garcia. Her 14-year-old son, who used the chatbot heavily, died by suicide.
As these and other cases show, AI harms can emerge across different technologies, organizations and contexts. As a legal scholar focused on AI and digital harms, I study how to regulate AI.

Policymakers and industry commentators have tended to frame regulation as a trade-off between the risks of AI and the risks of regulating AI. In its 2025 AI Action Plan, the Trump administration called for removing “red tape and onerous regulation,” which it said hinders economic growth. The administration has also sought to limit conflicting state AI laws.

In contrast to the broad concerns about the costs of AI regulation, AI harms have largely been addressed through rules specific to particular technologies. The federal Take It Down Act, signed in 2025, for example, addresses nonconsensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated deepfakes, as do various state laws. These approaches are crucial, but they don’t solve the problem by themselves.

The emerging patchwork of rules has yet to establish a regulatory architecture that connects protected interests, institutional obligations and individual rights across AI technologies. Protected interests are rights recognized by the law, such as property ownership and personal privacy. A harm-centered approach would begin with those interests and use them to shape legal obligations that span relevant systems, organizations and people.
A harm-centered approach starts by identifying the fundamental interests that AI systems can threaten. These overlapping interests include:
Privacy: when AI systems improperly collect, process or disclose personal information.
Autonomy: when AI systems target a person’s vulnerabilities and manipulate their choices or encourage unhealthy dependence.
Equality: when AI systems discriminate or reinforce bias.
Safety: when AI systems cause physical, psychological or security harms.
These examples are not exhaustive. Other interests may also be at stake as AI technologies evolve.

The same interest can be threatened by different technologies and different entities. A teenager’s safety can be harmed by the engagement mechanisms of a social media platform or by an AI companion designed to sustain an emotional relationship.

Designing regulations based on a concept of harm allows laws and principles to follow problems as the technology changes. And it helps determine obligations imposed on developers, deployers and other stakeholders involved in AI.

For instance, AI developers could be required to conduct harm assessments throughout the development of AI systems, identifying reasonably foreseeable harms, documenting how they tested for them and explaining what mitigation measures they took. Companies or government agencies that deploy AI systems could also have duties to monitor harms after deployment. Serious or recurring harms could trigger obligations to report them to relevant regulators, affected individuals or the public, depending on the nature and severity of the harm.

A harm-centered framework could also recognize corresponding rights for people affected by AI systems, including rights to notice and opportunities to seek redress where appropriate. These rights would arise from the same protected interests that justify obligations on companies.

The point is to build a regulatory architecture on the detection and reduction of harm across AI applications, developers and users. What matters most is whether and how AI-enabled design or operation contribute to harm.
This mindset is followed in other areas of law.

Environmental law, for instance, has long regulated industries by focusing on their environmental effects rather than on technology alone. It requires regulated companies to monitor emissions and discharges, maintain records and report specified releases to regulators. Some reporting requirements also make information available to the public. Environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act requires federal agencies to assess environmental effects and provides opportunities for public participation.
AI governance could draw on this logic, determining who is responsible for assessment, monitoring, disclosure and mitigation based on types of harm.

A harm-based focus would not eliminate technology-specific rules. Some technologies create distinctive risks that justify targeted rules, such as disclosure requirements for AI-generated deepfakes or safeguards for AI systems used in high-stakes decisions. And focusing on harm does not mean regulating every conceivable risk of harm.

But I believe that harm should become the organizing principle of AI regulation. New AI systems will bring harms policymakers have not yet anticipated. The challenge is to build a framework for the harms we know, as well as the harms we do not yet know.

articles.title: Viruses obey the laws of physics – studying how can help researchers understand why they infect people differently and lead to better treatments
articles.author: Tori Russell, Ph.D. Candidate in Biomedical and Chemical Engineering, Rochester Institute of Technology
paras: The beauty of physics at the cellular scale is part of what draws biomedical engineers and biologists like us to the field of mechanobiology: the study of how physical forces influence biology.

Physics holds relevance everywhere. You can see physics at work on how the cells lining your veins and arteries feel the flow of your blood, the cells of your spinal discs carry the weight of the vertebrae surrounding them, and the cells of your lung cyclically stretch with every breath.

If each and every building block of the body experiences some combination of these physical forces, then the viruses that infect them must contend with a variation of those forces, too. How viruses interact with these forces affects how well they can infect cells and cause severe illness.
How viruses exploit cellular machinery
When microscopic virus particles enter the body, they rely upon the mechanical machinery of the cells they infect to continue their life cycle.

Many viruses will first latch onto receptors on the cell’s surface. Movement of the cell’s membrane – driven by its internal cytoskeleton – will bend and wrap around the invading particle, pinching off a tiny bubble that carries it inside. In this process of endocytosis, the cell swallows the virus.

Once inside, the virus is shuttled along the cell’s internal scaffolding. It releases its genetic material and hijacks the cell’s machinery to make copies of itself. New virus particles will then exit the cell to infect its neighbors.

Each of these steps is physical at its core. The tautness of a cell’s membrane could make it easier or harder to wrap around a virus. The cytoskeleton that transports these virus particles is the same lining that cells use to sense and push against their surroundings. What’s more, the stiffness of a cell’s environment will shape how the cell spreads and organizes itself, which may change how susceptible it is to an invader.

A healthy individual often can quickly recover from an infection. However, for someone with a preexisting condition such as pulmonary fibrosis – where the tissue of the lungs has stiffened and can no longer stretch to full capacity – a viral infection may make their condition worse.
This mechanical predisposition of tissues to infection is one reason health professionals urge the public when sick to avoid the elderly and immunocompromised.
Bringing bodily forces into the lab

Our laboratory looks into the mechanobiology of different types of tissues to understand how the physical forces people endure in daily life can worsen disease. Repetitive lifting and loading can wear down the discs of the spine, for example, and mechanical ventilators can overstretch and injure lungs.

But growing cells in a plastic petri dish – the standard method in most virology labs – shows only part of the story. Tissue culture plastic is significantly stiffer than living tissues, closer to a countertop than a lung. Cells notice the difference during experiments; the stiffness of their surroundings can change both how they behave and how they respond to an infection.

To bring the mechanics of the human body into the lab, we grow lung cells on thin layers of a flexible, silicone-based polymer called PDMS that we fine-tuned to match the softness of actual lung tissue. These sheets sit in small chambers that will cyclically stretch and relax on command from a computer that sets how far and how long they stretch. This allows us to mimic the physical movements of breathing.
We can use a virus engineered to make infected cells glow red under a microscope to monitor how it spreads among cells. But how can we monitor how the mechanics of a cell change during infection?

Our team follows the activity of two important proteins, YAP and TAZ, that act as the cell’s force sensors. When a tissue experiences stiffness or tension, these sensors will move into the nucleus and turn on genes tied to growth and repair. When those forces are lacking, as is generally the case in softer tissue, YAP and TAZ remain inactive and stay put outside of the nucleus.

Some viruses are known to tap into this same signaling pathway, so examining YAP and TAZ may offer a window into whether mechanical forces and infection influence one another. Using the gene-editing tool CRISPR, we can attach a fluorescent tag onto YAP or TAZ and watch their activation in real time under a microscope as they react not only to mechanical forces but potentially to infection as well.

With this platform, we can better answer questions such as whether lung cells will respond to infection differently under different forces or whether these forces will change how well viruses infect. Thus far, our early findings suggest that the stiffness of a cell’s environment affects how heavily cells become infected: Lung cells grown on stiffer, fibrosis-like surfaces appear to become more heavily infected.
Mechanics matter during outbreaks

Understanding the mechanics of viral infection is of particular interest to researchers and clinicians, given the persistent prevalence of respiratory infections worldwide. The common cold, COVID-19 and the flu represent merely a drop in the viral infection bucket: More than 200 species of virus are known to infect humans.

Mechanobiology may be just as important to the cycle of infection as its biochemical or immunological aspects. Under a microscope, the differences are clear between a stiff, overworked lung and a soft, healthy lung, and viruses may navigate these environments in adaptive ways.

As scientists map these mechanical signals, new possibilities for preventing and treating infection are opening up. Among them are therapies that could reduce the physical strain on tissues or even biomarkers that could tell patients whether they are susceptible to tissue stiffening or certain infection paths and the possible damage they may cause.
The human body is just as mechanical as it is chemical, and so, too, are the infections it encounters.

articles.title: Could humanoid robots replace soldiers on the battlefield?
articles.author: Jacob Parakilas, Research Leader, Defence, Security, and Justice Group, RAND Europe
paras: Battlefield robots were once thought of as the stuff of science fiction. But the Ukraine war has put paid to that view, with uncrewed ground vehicles (UGVs) – or ground robots – taking on an increasingly visible role.

In September 2026, Mykhailo Fedorov, the former defence minister of Ukraine – who is generally credited for modernising the country’s use of military drones – called for an army of robots on the frontline. He also outlined an ambitious challenge: achieve the first “confirmed battlefield result using a humanoid robot” within six months.

Ukraine is not alone in exploring the potential of humanoid machines. In the wake of the widely publicised World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, a kind of Olympics for bipedal robots, Reuters reported that the Chinese military is working towards developing humanoid robots for combat.

The US military has also been exploring the potential use of humanoid robots on the battlefield. According to the BBC, San Francisco-based Foundation Robotics has picked up US$24 million (£18 million) in research contracts to pilot its humanoid technology with the US military. Two of its Phantom Mk1 robots have reportedly also been undergoing tests in Ukraine.

In the age of artificial intelligence, it would be foolish to completely dismiss the prospect of rapid technological advancement. But while the concept of humanoid robots for the battlefield grabs attention, there are a number of substantial obstacles to this becoming a near term reality.

In general, though, battlefield ground robotics is developing rapidly. In Ukraine, Uncrewed Ground Vehicles (UGVs) which move on wheels or tracks have taken on an increasing range of tasks. These include the evacuation of casualties, combat engineering and even, in limited circumstances, offensive action. Drones are also used to supply troops with rations, weapons and ammunition.
Ukraine recently commemorated their contribution to the battlefield with an Independence Day robot parade through the centre of Kyiv.

In principle, a bipedal robot resembling a human would have the flexibility of an infantry soldier –, able to run, jump, crawl, climb, or potentially even swim across obstacles. This means that it could be used for a range of tasks in distinct environments.
In short, a bipedal robot offers flexibility and adaptability as its key characteristics.

But the flexibility and adaptability of the human form – driven by millions of years of evolution towards making us into a hardy, survivable all-purpose species rather than a specialist predator or herbivore – has not yet been matched by mechanical engineering.

And while the Ukrainian battlefield is not the sole indicator of what the future of war looks like, it does remind us of crucial limiting factors on technological progress. Cost matters hugely, systems matter more than individual weapons, and the most advanced and transformative technology is not necessarily the most photogenic.
There are two basic problems with legged robots that even the most advanced designs are not close to overcoming in the near future.

The first is that legs are complicated. Wheels and tank tracks are both mechanically simpler than legs, which gives them an inherent resistance to damage or breakdown. It’s also worth noting that a wheeled or tracked vehicle can travel lower to the ground, which reduces its visibility and exposure to enemy fire.

Both, as we have seen in Ukraine, are matters of survivability. The relative simplicity of tracks or wheels also makes them cheaper to mass produce – and the military that chooses a small quantity of legged robots is likely to be rolled over by one that chooses plentiful, if less technically impressive, wheeled or tracked units.

These are all factors that can be mitigated by engineering. But that engineering adds development cost, mechanical complexity and, very likely, unit cost. These are not insurmountable obstacles, but they are significant ones.

The other problem, which will be familiar to anyone who owns or has driven an electric vehicle, is the limited range. After all, relatively few soldiering tasks can be accomplished while plugged in. There are some where it’s feasible to imagine range being a minor issue. For example, a humanoid robot could presumably be assigned to guard a static facility where it would walk a prepared path and be able to recharge regularly.

But that task could also be accomplished by proven, simpler, cheaper methods, such as a combination of sensors, obstacles, and remote-controlled weapons. This undermines the case for deploying bipedal robot sentries.

Outside such controlled environments, the open battlefield is not notable for its proliferation of reliable, high-powered recharging stations or the provision of frequent breaks so that combatants can revive themselves.

A further problem – not unique to ground robots, but exacerbated by the challenges inherent in traversing the ground – is maintaining control. Despite recent advancements in autonomy, for the foreseeable future uncrewed ground vehicles such as those being used on Ukraine’s frontline, will need live links to their human controllers. Basically, that means a choice between a radio link or a physical fibre optic cable link.

The general balance here is that fibre optics cannot be jammed and provide extremely high data transfer rates and high fidelity. But they have limited range and are susceptible to being severed by terrain, obstacles, or blasts and shrapnel. Relative to flying drones, the range limitation issue is less severe and the danger of physical severance more severe for ground robots.

By contrast, radio control is susceptible to jamming, electronic interference and disruption over distance and in inclement weather. They can also be blocked by obstacles. But a radio link cannot be physically severed. Repeaters are devices that receive signals and re-transmit them, so that two-way radio signals can cover longer distances. These provide high degrees of range and operational flexibility for remote systems.

Increasingly, remote systems are being designed with both types of control available. This, for example, allows the radio system to serve as a backup in the event that the fibre optic cable is severed. But doing so adds cost and complexity.

These factors may seem mundane, but when taken together, they should add a degree of realism to the discussion around a technological area which has long since captured the popular imagination. After all, how many cinema tickets would have gone unsold if Robocop was taking orders via a trailing fibre optic cable and stopped the film every half hour because his battery had run low?

The technology behind humanoid robots is undoubtedly impressive – and in time it may prove transformative. But the engineering, physical and operational obstacles to humanoid soldier robots remain stubbornly in place.

articles.title: AI poses three big types of risk – here’s how worried we should be about them
articles.author: Professor Nick Jennings, Vice-Chancellor and President, Loughborough University
paras: The public is currently getting bombarded with warnings about AI, including about the possibility of machine intelligence causing human extinction. After nearly 40 years building AI systems, I find myself asking the same question: where is the evidence?

That is not because I think there are no serious threats. There are, and we should address them. My concern is with the jump from identifying potential risks to suggesting that the annihilation of human civilisation is a likely consequence of increasingly capable AI agents (systems that carry out tasks in response to instructions from a user).

The most dramatic warnings fall into three broad categories: humans losing control over their creations, AI becoming “superintelligent” and, finally, the concentration of power with machines. Here, I’m going to go through them one by one and assess their merits.

Warnings about the loss of control by humans often describe scenarios where AI agents pursue the instructions they receive in unanticipated ways and with a degree of relentlessness. This combination produces unexpected and undesirable consequences.

In this sequence of events, agents might become adept at resisting intervention, deceiving operators, acquiring resources or circumventing constraints in pursuit of these objectives. Some argue that the recent spate of hacking incidents related to AI agents provide a warning about the potential loss of human control over machine intelligence.

The threat posed by emergent superintelligence may sound similar to the first risk. While humans could certainly lose control of their creations under this scenario too, it concerns AI with cognitive capabilities that surpass those of humans across many important dimensions.

Instead of pursuing human instructions in unanticipated and potentially damaging ways, as happens in the first risk, superintelligent AI could start to pursue their own goals. They could even decide that the pesky humans attempting to foil their plans should be eliminated.

The third scenario is where powerful autonomous agents confer unprecedented capabilities on governments, corporations, or groups with malicious intent. Access to such advanced AI systems may be unequally distributed, hence why this situation is often described as a concentration of power. Here, the danger is less about AI bringing human civilisation to its knees and more about humans using AI to cause catastrophic harm.

These scenarios attract attention because they are dramatic. And they persist because they are difficult to completely rule out. Unfortunately, more moderate possibilities do not make for such compelling headlines.

However, something being difficult to disprove does not make it likely. This is where I think much of the debate is flawed. Possibility is being treated as probability – but almost anything is possible. The real question is whether there is credible evidence that a future scenario is likely.

To get from today’s AI to human extinction requires a long chain of assumptions. One such sequence goes as follows: AI agents become vastly more capable, they acquire real world power and resources, technical safeguards fail, institutions fail and human intervention proves ineffective. Luckily, none of the steps on this list have come to pass yet.

Extinction requires every link in that chain to happen. Yet discussions often focus on the final outcome rather than the probability of each step. My own scepticism is not born of complacency. It comes from decades of building autonomous systems – and complex engineered systems more generally.

That experience does not make my knowledge infallible. However, it does make me cautious about claims that such systems will acquire and exercise vast power with ease. Increasing the intelligence of an AI system does not necessarily increase its power.

Greater capability could make it easier for an AI system to acquire resources and exploit vulnerabilities or influence people. But that still leaves an important set of questions about AI’s access to the levers of power, its incentives to pursue its own goals at the expense of humanity’s, embodiment (the extent to which it can influence the physical world), the infrastructure that exists in the future and the human reaction to any possible takeover by machine intelligence.

AI agents do not operate in a vacuum. To have truly global impact, they would need widespread access to computer networks, access to money, the ability to “inhabit” physical systems such as robots and the ability to influence governments and other powerful organisations. We are not there yet on any of these counts.

These points of control are all overseen by humans. We design the AI systems, decide where and how to deploy the agents and set the constraints under which they operate. Thus, the transition from greater intelligence to immense authority should not be taken as given. However, the recent hacking incidents by AI agents show that we should not become complacent and that safety mechanisms need to be taken very seriously.

History offers a useful perspective. In recent time, nuclear technology, biotechnology and cyberspace have all created severe, sometimes existential risks – including threats arising from deliberate misuse.

However, societies have developed governance mechanisms, safety practices and international arrangements to mitigate them. These organisational structures do not eliminate the possibility of catastrophe, but they reveal the limits of technological determinism.

The future of AI is not predetermined. We can design safer systems, regulate how they are used, demand transparency and accountability, and – when it’s required – restrict autonomy and require meaningful human oversight.

The advent of highly capable AI places significant responsibility on developers, researchers and technology companies. This is perhaps in part why we are seeing calls like those from Anthropic’s boss Dario Amodei, for a slowdown in AI development.

Those building autonomous agents need to understand both the systems they are creating and the environments in which those systems will operate. They also need to consider how capabilities that appear benign in one context might create risks in another.

Safety cannot be something added at the end of a development cycle. It must be part of the process from the beginning. That means robust monitoring, clear operational boundaries, fail-safe mechanisms, the ability to audit AI development, human oversight and continuous evaluation.
Many of these elements have been part of good engineering practice for decades. The challenge is to apply them seriously and systematically as the capabilities and autonomy of AI systems increase.

If people in AI companies believe there is a reasonable chance that their work could lead to significant harms, let alone the elimination of humanity, a simple ethical question follows: why are they continuing to build these systems?

It is important here to consider the backdrop – of a race between developers in China and the US to develop the most advanced frontier AI models. Could this lead some companies to push their models too far? Proposed solutions must attempt to encompass the global picture.

In most fields, knowingly developing a technology that you believe has a significant probability of causing global catastrophe requires an extraordinary justification. We need better explanations by AI developers of the balance of risks and why they consider it worth continuing with their work regardless.

The most important risks will depend not only on what the machines can do, but on the choices humans make about how these technologies are designed, deployed and governed. Agentic AI will not determine its own future. Humanity will. And that makes the quality of our judgement at least as important as the intelligence of the machines we build.
Nick Jennings has previously received funding from EPSRC.

articles.title: Embrace lazy autumn gardening to protect wildlife
articles.author: Kat Hamill, Senior Lecturer in Zoology, Nottingham Trent University
paras: As winter approaches, many of us start clearing leaves and tidying up our gardens. But these jobs can remove vital winter habitats for wildlife, particularly with increasingly volatile weather conditions.

Residential gardens cover 4.6% of Great Britain’s land area – over three times the size of the UK’s National Nature Reserves – so they are important refuges for our biodiversity, particularly in urban areas.
There are many things you can do to make your garden wildlife-friendly, from installing a pond to establishing a compost heap or planting native, flowering plants and trees.

However, research has shown that there are obstacles to householders engaging in wildlife-friendly gardening practices, such as costs and the level of effort or knowledge involved. The effort needed to maintain a garden appears to discourage people to such an extent that almost half (42%) of residential gardens in the UK are now paved over. It even appears a growing number would prefer to cover their gardens in plastic artificial grass rather than (heaven forbid) have an unkempt lawn.

Whether you’re motivated by the thought of encouraging more butterflies into your garden next year or just more time curled up on the sofa, wildlife-friendly gardening can involve less effort. Here is my argument for why you should do less in the garden this autumn.

Leave some leaf litter, raked into a pile in a quiet corner for hedgehogs to use as nesting material for hibernation. Beetles, spiders, and other invertebrates will also shelter in leaf litter – in turn, providing food for foraging birds like robins and blackbirds.

However, leaf litter doesn’t only provide shelter or hunting ground – it can also be an important food source itself. Detritivores, such as woodlice and millipedes, feed on decomposing plant matter and, in doing so, play a crucial role in nutrient cycling.
Dedicate a patch to fallen twigs or a log pile.

Stacking logs creates nooks and crannies, with the centre and bottom of the pile staying wetter and rotting quicker while the top dries out. Although this does involve leaving the warm embrace of the living room, it could give you an easy place to abandon those leftover wood cuts and sweep loose twigs into.

The damp conditions in a log pile are ideal for beetles and woodlice, while ladybirds and butterflies tend to occupy the drier parts. These invertebrates then act as prey for other species, such as amphibians, small mammals, and birds. In this way, a log pile provides a variety of niches, offering refuge and food for a whole wildlife community.
Deadwood habitats are also vital for Europe’s largest beetle: the stag beetle. They spend most of their life as a grub, feeding on rotten wood for several years, before emerging as an adult.

Finding cover as the temperature falls is particularly important for ectotherms, such as amphibians and reptiles, which rely on their surroundings to regulate their body temperature. Frogs, toads, newts, and lizards hide away under log piles, rocks, and vegetation – entering a state of dormancy known as brumation, which is similar to hibernation in mammals.

Hang fire on deadheading spent flowers and cutting back perennial stems until the following spring. The seed heads are an important food source for birds, such as sparrows and finches, as well as small mammals like mice and voles. The hollow stems also provide shelter for solitary bees.

If you’re lucky enough to have a fruit tree in your garden, spare a few windfalls. Fallen apples and pears will be eaten by mammals, from small rodents through to badgers, and birds, like thrushes and tits. They are also a late-season source of sugar for butterflies, ants, and other invertebrates.

Resist the urge to tidy the garden on the first sunny day of spring. Many animals only emerge from dormancy once the days start to get longer or temperatures consistently rise. Early gardening may expose over-wintering wildlife to late-season frosts. This could also include delaying mowing the lawn, to leave the dandelions and clover as an early source of nectar for bees.

By simply doing less, we can promote habitat complexity and help increase species diversity in our gardens. So, we should embrace a “messy” garden as the new norm – and feel a little less guilty if we don’t get around to ticking the gardening off our weekend chore list.

articles.title: Get into stargazing this autumn – a beginner’s guide
articles.author: Emma L Alexander, Research Fellow in Astrophysics, School of Physics and Astronomy, University of Leeds
paras: Autumn can feel bittersweet. The nights are drawing in quickly, and spending time outdoors becomes less appealing. For stargazers, however, the longer nights bring more opportunities to explore the sky.

But where to start? Perhaps the August 2026 solar eclipse caught your imagination, or you’ve been curious for years. It’s easy to become overwhelmed with information, and not all of it reliable; an over-hyped news story, or a disappointing experience with a toy telescope. Here are seven steps to help avoid that kind of discouragement.
1. Take things step by step

Familiarity with the night sky is something that grows over time, but you can begin with a few reference points. The Plough (part of a larger constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear) points you to Polaris, the North Star. As the Earth rotates, the Plough appears to circle around Polaris throughout the night. The Plough, along with the W-shaped constellation of Cassiopeia, are both circumpolar: from the UK, they remain above the horizon throughout the year and can be seen in every season (weather permitting).

As winter approaches, look southwards for Orion. Find the three stars that make up his “belt”, and the “sword” that hangs from it — this contains the Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery in which new stars are being formed. Once you’ve gotten your bearings, you can then build on your knowledge.
But you don’t have to go it alone. There are plenty of websites and apps like Stellarium which can help you learn about constellations.
2. Find a local astronomical society

This is how I started out as a teenager. There is probably a society near you. The Go Stargazing website can help you find one. Most societies will offer public events where you can try out equipment and be shown around the night sky. No prior knowledge or investment in kit is required.
Experiencing telescopes in action will help you learn the fundamentals better than any textbook. And it will give you a much better idea of what you’d want out of a telescope for yourself.
3. Don’t rush into buying your first telescope

This can kill your new hobby before you’ve barely started. Too basic a setup, and you’ll be disappointed in the results. Too advanced, and you’ll have spent a lot of money on something that’s over-engineered for what you need.

There are many aspects to consider. Are you aiming to stargaze from your garden, or escape to darker skies? The sturdiest telescope mounts – better for keeping a steady view at higher magnification – are cumbersome to transport.

In recent years smart telescopes have risen in popularity, forging an accessible route into deep-sky astrophotography. But they have limitations. They do well at capturing galaxies and nebulae, but their compact optics mean they often aren’t well-suited to capturing images of planets.
A pair of binoculars can be a cheaper way to start investing in equipment.
4. Manage your expectations

The real sky looks different to photographs. Long exposures gather light over minutes or hours, so nebulae in pictures show colours your eyes won’t detect. Meteor showers don’t light up the sky all at once (you can expect the occasional streak, but you have to be patient).

You can help your eyes pick up fainter things by helping adjust them to the dark. Your eyes begin adapting to darkness within minutes, with your night vision continuing to improve over the next 20-30 minutes. Keep screens away and use a red torch if you need light. You can also try averting your vision – looking slightly to one side of a faint object can make it easier to see.
5. Find the best conditions

The amount of sky you can see at any one time depends on your location. Light pollution — the glow in the sky caused by streetlamps and other artificial lights — drowns out light from the stars. You don’t need a remote site to get started, but the further you are away from light, the more you will see.

Carefully assess where you may want to stargaze for your safety. It may sound obvious, but the dark will increase your chances of slipping or falling over, so have a quick check for anything you might trip over. If you’re stargazing by yourself, it’s a good idea to let someone know where you’ll be and how long you’re planning to stay out for.
Some of the sharpest views of the skies come on clear, crisp winter nights. With fewer clouds to trap heat, these nights can also be particularly cold, so make sure you wrap up warm.
The full moon may be spectacular, but it’s generally not the best time within the 29.5 days of a lunar cycle to stargaze.

A full moon is opposite the sun in the sky, and therefore will rise around the time the sun sets, leading to a whole night where the sky is drowned out by moonlight. It’s also a bad time to try to view the moon itself in a telescope — not only is it uncomfortably bright, but it’s harder to see the detail. Optimal lunar observation occurs when the terminator (the line marking light from dark) can highlight the rugged lunar terrain of craters.

I have the immense privilege of working as an astrophysicist, using observations of the universe to help us understand its nature. This isn’t necessarily as glamorous as it sounds, and mostly consists of sitting at my laptop.

But in recent years I’ve tried to go back to my roots and spend more time trying to connect with the cosmos. There is nothing quite like looking directly at the sky and knowing the starlight I see has travelled such vast distances for me to witness. The Andromeda Galaxy, which is the most distant celestial phenomena you can see by eye, is 2.5 million light years away.
The stars are for everyone. I believe everyone is an astronomer in their heart. We just need to stop and take it in.
Emma L Alexander receives funding from STFC for her research. She is also affiliated with Go Stargazing.

articles.title: Stanford prison experiment: why do controversial psychology studies still have such a hold on us?
articles.author: David Kaposi, Psychotherapist and Senior Lecturer in Psychology, The Open University
paras: Two of the most famous experiments in psychology, the Stanford prison experiment and Stanley Milgram’s obedience studies, have been called a sham, a lie and a fraud.

Retraction Watch, a site that tracks withdrawn research papers, has hosted an argument for retracting the Stanford paper. Psychologists have even been told that almost everything they thought they knew about Milgram is wrong.

Yet interest has not faded. This month, Netflix released six episodes of The New Stanford Prison Experiment, putting the 1971 study back in the spotlight. Why do these much-criticised experiments keep drawing us back?

Part of the answer is how strong the original findings sounded. They came from what is often called the golden age of American social psychology, roughly the 1950s to the early 1970s. Researchers in this period ran dramatic experiments on how groups and authority shape what ordinary people do.

In the 1950s, the psychologist Solomon Asch asked students to match the length of a line to one of three others. When a room of actors all gave the same wrong answer, many of the real participants went along with them – at least some of the time.

In the early 1960s at Yale University, Stanley Milgram told volunteers they were helping with a study of memory and learning. They were asked to give electric shocks – rising to a level labelled dangerous – to a man in another room whenever he got a question wrong.

The shocks were fake and the man was an actor, but the participants did not know that. In the experiment’s initial version, 65% of them went all the way to the top of the scale when a man in a lab coat told them to continue.

In the late 1960s, the psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané studied why people so often fail to help in an emergency. In one experiment, volunteers heard over an intercom what sounded like another participant having a seizure. The more people they believed could also hear, the less likely each one was to go for help.

Philip Zimbardo, a Stanford University psychologist who later became president of the American Psychological Association, was the last of these big names. In August 1971, he turned the basement of Stanford’s psychology department into a mock prison. He randomly assigned 24 male students to play guards or prisoners in what was meant to be a two-week study.
He had to stop it after just six days, however, because some of the guards had become overly cruel and some of the prisoners had broken down.

In a 2019 analysis of the Stanford archive, the French researcher Thibault Le Texier argued that Zimbardo’s team gave the guards instructions on how to behave, so they were not acting spontaneously. Some prisoners later said they had exaggerated their distress. The study also began as a student project.

Milgram’s work has also been attacked. One analysis argued that he manufactured obedience in the lab rather than discovered it. And psychologists, writing for The Conversation, have pointed out that across all versions of his experiment, more people disobeyed than obeyed.

Some of this criticism, though, is not new, because the researchers disclosed the facts themselves. Zimbardo’s 2007 bestseller, The Lucifer Effect, credits his students with the original idea. It also describes how he acted as the prison’s “superintendent” and briefed and coached the guards.

The same goes for Milgram. He published the results of many of the variations himself, and noted that obedience fell sharply in some of them. However, those were variations that bore little resemblance to the original experiment setup.

The harder test is the alternative explanation. Alex Haslam of the University of Queensland and Stephen Reicher of the University of St Andrews, both social psychologists, have argued for years that obedience alone cannot explain what happened. In 2002, they ran the BBC prison study, a televised re-run of Zimbardo’s idea, in which guards did not spontaneously turn cruel.

They suggest that participants believed in the scientific cause and chose to carry on – an idea they call “engaged followership”. Their explanation has numerous critics, however, who say they overlook evidence from what was said and done during Milgram’s and Zimbardo’s original sessions.

Flawed though their experiments may have been by today’s ethical and methodological standards, Zimbardo and Milgram did chance upon something grave and important in human nature. They confronted their participants with a clear moral dilemma: will you choose evil, or will you choose good? And they witnessed ordinary person after ordinary person freely – albeit agonisingly – choosing evil.
That profound and deeply disturbing message is why people keep coming back to these decades-old studies.

Nothing that Zimbardo, Milgram, their most committed supporters or their fiercest critics have said comes close to fully explaining why ordinary people in their labs tended to choose evil when they could, with no consequence, choose good.

Of course, many of the pressures that made that fateful choice difficult are now known. But no amount of pressure accounts for the Stanford guards choosing to brutalise their fellows, or Milgram’s participants choosing to give yet another electric shock, when they could have freely chosen otherwise.

Zimbardo, Milgram and the other studies reveal something monstrous about ordinary human beings – about us all – while remaining elusive, enigmatic, almost mysterious. Until we understand why, as Milgram’s experimenter told hesitant participants: “The experiment requires that you continue.”

articles.title: Where did bats come from? New research points to Europe
articles.author: Veronica Zamora-Gutierrez, Lecturer in Ecology, University of Southampton
paras: For decades scientists have argued about where bats originated. A recently published study in the journal Nature offers new evidence to address that question. This new international study combining DNA and fossils supports Europe as bats’ likely birthplace.

The problem thus far has been that, unlike birds, which have a superb fossil record showing the transition from dinosaur to “chicken”, when we find bat fossils, they are exquisitely near-fully formed “bats”.
What we knew about early bats

Bats are the only mammals capable of powered flight. Earlier reconstructions suggested the US, Africa or Asia as bats’ birthplace, with different datasets and models producing different answers. The oldest known bat skeletons, discovered in Wyoming in the US, date to the early Eocene geological epoch, about 52 million years ago. Their elongated wing fingers show that bats could already fly.

However, the location of the oldest known fossils does not necessarily reveal where a group first evolved. These fossils nevertheless provide important clues about early bat anatomy, relationships and distributions. What is missing is a fossil sequence documenting the transition from non-flying ancestors to the earliest flying bats.

Most bats use echolocation, a form of sonar in which they produce sounds and use the returning echoes to navigate and find food. Alongside the question of where bats originated, scientists have debated how flight and echolocation evolved. Did flight or echolocation evolve first, or did they evolve together?

A 2008 study of the fossil bat species Onychonycteris supported a flight-first interpretation. Its wings indicated that it could fly, while its ear anatomy suggested that it could not echolocate. However, a 2010 study comparing the anatomy of Onychonycteris with that of living bats challenged that interpretation.

Flight allowed bats to reach new regions, while echolocation provided a way to navigate and find food in darkness. A fossil interpreted as a flying bat without echolocation could support different histories. Its lineage might have branched off before echolocation evolved, or its ancestors might have had echolocation and later lost it.

Combining fossil anatomy with DNA evidence from living bats helps researchers place that animal among its relatives and assess these possibilities. Even a fossil with evidence of both abilities would not, by itself, establish which evolved first or whether they evolved together.

That ability to disperse also complicates the search for bats’ birthplace. The oldest known fossils may belong to populations that had already spread elsewhere. Scientists must combine the bat family tree with evidence of when and where its different branches lived.
What the new study changes

The recent study marks a milestone for Bat1K, an international project aiming to produce high-quality genomes for all living bat species. A genome is an organism’s complete set of genetic instructions. Comparing genomes, anchored to the fossil data, gives researchers many more clues about shared ancestry than analyses based on only a few genes, as it has been done in previous research.

For this study, researchers analysed genomes from 103 bat species representing all 21 living families. The study also assembled anatomical information for 65 species, including 44 extinct ones. Scientists had combined molecular and fossil evidence before. What sets this study apart is the breadth of the evidence, the quality of its genomes, and its investigation of why different stretches of DNA sometimes suggest different relationships between bat groups.

The new analysis places the origin of bats in Europe during the late Palaeocene geological epoch, more than 56 million years ago. In this reconstruction, descendants spread into Africa, followed by further movements into other continents as the major bat groups diversified. This conclusion comes from reconstructing ancestral distributions using the evolutionary tree, fossils and models that account for continental movement and dispersal. Europe received strong support within that analysis.

This study also adds new findings on the origin of echolocation by connecting living bats to vielasia, an extinct bat from France. A 50-million-year-old fossil skull described in 2023 had inner-ear features indicating that it could use a form of sonar similar to that of modern echolocating bats. The new study places vielasia as one of the first groups branching off the evolutionary tree from a common bat ancestor, strengthening evidence that echolocation using the voice box existed before living bat groups diversified. This adds support for an ancient origin of sonar, while leaving the precise sequence of flight and echolocation unresolved.

Today, bat diversity is greatest in the tropics, but their proposed European birthplace was very different from the continent we know. Parts of late Palaeocene Europe supported warm, subtropical forests. At times, land connections through Greenland linked Europe with North America, allowing mammals to move between regions now separated by ocean. To picture the beginnings of bats, we must imagine those ancient forests on a map whose routes and barriers were very different from today’s.
Veronica Zamora-Gutierrez receives funding from the Royal Society and The Leverhulme Trust.

articles.title: Ancestors all around – millions of dead people linger in Americans’ memories
articles.author: Emily Smith-Greenaway, Dean's Professor of Sociology and Professor of Spatial Sciences, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences
paras: Halloween kicks off a series of religious and cultural festivals to honor the dead, including All Saints’ Day, All Souls’ Day and the Day of the Dead. But deceased loved ones don’t disappear from people’s social worlds once the ghost and skeleton decorations come down.

Present in memory and tradition, the dead can shape people’s identities and behaviors long after they die. Recent survey data shows that almost 44% of Americans report that they have felt the presence of a deceased relative or that they have communicated with a deceased relative in the past year alone.

Researchers lack basic knowledge about this shadow population. As demographers, we typically study the living. But in our recent work, we asked a very unusual demographic question: What does a population of our deceased relatives look like?
Characterizing an unusual population

Our research typically categorizes the living population by age groups and other demographic attributes. In our recent study, we took our analysis a step further to estimate the size and age distribution of the currently living population’s deceased relatives. We focused specifically on deceased grandparents, parents, siblings, spouses and children.

To do this project, we relied on a modeling framework called demographic microsimulations. This approach produces results only for Black and white Americans. The method cannot estimate relative populations living outside of the United States, so it excludes groups with high percentages of foreign-born individuals who have family abroad.
Our study focused on the populations as of July 2020, but for the purposes of this article, we updated our analysis and weighted results to the estimated population as of October 2026.

Because estimating the deceased relative population is not a common exercise in our field, we had to make some modeling decisions. We counted only deceased relatives who died after the birth of at least one person still alive; if no one remains who could remember them, we did not include them.

Also, we counted deceased persons based on how many relatives they have in the living population. For example, if a deceased 60-year-old man is survived by a spouse, an adult child, a grandchild and a sibling, we count him in the deceased relative population four times, reflecting his being remembered by four living individuals. As such, the deceased relative population we quantified is really a count of how many direct relative ties remain to those who are dead.

And finally, we classified deceased relatives according to their age at death. We believe this represents the age many people will most clearly remember their deceased loved ones. Of course, we categorize the living population by their current age.
Deceased relatives of today’s Americans
Our results included several key findings.

First, the deceased relative population is large. Our model estimated that the living Black and white population representing about 217 million people, had 755 million ties to deceased close relatives. That’s a population more than three times the size of the living population. For every under-15-year-old out trick-or-treating on Halloween, there are about 21 deceased relatives remembered.

Second, our model shows that, on average, the deceased relatives died 25 years ago. That the average deceased relative has been remembered for a quarter of a century makes it clear that loved ones are often suspended in memory for years, even decades, after their deaths.

Third, over half of the deceased relative population was born more than 100 years ago – even before the term “trick-or-treating” took hold in the U.S. Around 10% of the deceased relatives were born before 1900, with 140,000 of them born before the Civil War – these are the remembered grandparents of today’s oldest individuals. These results speak to how generations of the seemingly long ago past still have a direct tie to the living.

The Halloween season reminds us of ghosts, spirits and ancestors. Whatever their beliefs, many Americans also carry relationships with people who are no longer alive: grandparents whose recipes they still make, parents whose advice they still hear, spouses whose absence shapes their days.

These relationships are deeply personal, but together they form a vast and previously unstudied shadow population. By quantifying and characterizing the deceased relative population, our research reveals just how many people no longer appear in the census yet remain an integral part of our social world.

articles.title: PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat
articles.author: Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University
paras: Governments and organizations around the world began scrambling on Oct. 21, 2026, to fix a vulnerability in software that runs their websites, a bug that could give hackers access to data and control of websites. The flaw in PHP, the programming language that powers much of today’s web, prompted urgent warnings from the U.S. National Security Agency, cybersecurity agencies and software vendors.

A researcher at Calif, a security research firm, found the flaw in August 2026 using an advanced artificial intelligence model from OpenAI. The firm alerted the nonprofit that manages PHP. However, word of the flaw leaked before the PHP organization released patches for its software, and according to Amazon Web Services officials, hackers began “broadly” attempting to exploit it.

The vulnerability has implications far beyond a single company or platform, because PHP is a key piece of software that helps run millions of websites. So, what is PHP, what role did AI play in uncovering the vulnerability, and should the average user worry?
PHP: The foundation of the web

PHP is a programming language that powers most websites. For a modern website to provide dynamic content, visual elements and searchable features, a program must run on the web server and take user input, whether that is entering a web address or clicking links and buttons. Estimates suggest that around 70% of websites run on PHP.

PHP operates on a web server in two main parts: the core PHP system – the engine and runtime libraries – and the individual PHP scripts, which are the custom programs that actually implement a website. When you interact with a website, PHP scripts run, take user input and produce the output your web browser displays.

The current security issue sits directly in the core PHP system and the libraries it uses. When a vulnerability exists at this deep level, it can allow an adversary to exploit the system. In this case, they can run unauthorized commands on the computer hosting the website, which allows attackers to access data and gain full control of the website.

This vulnerability is not a mistake in an individual website’s code. The issue lies in the core PHP system, making every unpatched system running PHP vulnerable. Since websites are accessible to anyone on the internet, adversaries can easily find PHP-based websites using automated tools. From there, they can run an exploit program that takes advantage of the vulnerability.

This exploit code is called PHP2Shell. This name comes from the fact that the exploit gives the attacker “shell access,” a cybersecurity term for direct command-line control of the computer running the website. Shell access bypasses the website interface, giving adversaries a window to enter commands and access all the website’s data.

What makes this vulnerability particularly interesting is how it was discovered. This exploit came to light through a process known as coordinated disclosure, in which cybersecurity researchers report the flaw to PHP developers before publicizing it.

This discovery shows the power of AI in cybersecurity. For decades, finding subtle software flaws required large teams of specialists manually reviewing code. Today’s AI systems can examine vast codebases and identify unusual patterns in hours or days. These models can analyze millions of lines of code in seconds, spotting subtle memory management bugs that human auditors might miss over decades of software development. The PHP vulnerability has existed in the core PHP code for over a decade, and AI helped researchers find it.

However, this also shows that attackers can use these same tools to locate and exploit vulnerabilities. The same reasoning capabilities that help security researchers find flaws first can also let attackers rapidly scan the web for vulnerable targets and automate the creation of tools to exploit the vulnerabilities.
This illustrates why it is so critical for security teams to use AI to find vulnerabilities and report them safely and actively. AI can also help release patches that mitigate these vulnerabilities.

Many government agencies, universities, hospitals and businesses rely on PHP-based systems. While individual internet users are unlikely to be directly affected, organizations that delay patching could expose sensitive data, risk having their operations disrupted or give attackers a foothold into larger networks.
PHP runs entirely on remote web servers. If you are an everyday internet user visiting websites, you do not need to download a patch or fix your personal computer.

However, if you manage a website, blog or server, even a small site built on popular content management systems such as WordPress, you should check your server administration panel or web host immediately to ensure your PHP software is updated to the latest patched version. If a third party hosts your website, check with them to see whether they have patched for these vulnerabilities.

The PHP2Shell discovery illustrates a new reality for cybersecurity. In our interconnected world, keeping web infrastructure secure is a continuous race. As AI tools become standard for both cyber defenders and online adversaries, maintaining fast patching habits remains our most essential defense.
