articles.title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
articles.author: Monique Mitchell Turner, Professor of Communication, Michigan State University
paras: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen.

The ad ran as a paid spot only once, in support of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s reelection campaign. It never mentioned his opponent, republican Barry Goldwater. The ad played on a fear voters already held, that Goldwater might start a nuclear war. Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the uproar got it rebroadcast in full on network news.

I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their reactions to political ads to how anxiety drives people to seek out, and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats.
The LBJ “Daisy” ad shows why political campaigns to this day continue to reach for fear, and it hints at why the payoff is less predictable than you might think.
Fear is an alarm. It tells you something threatening is close. You feel scared when you believe you are at risk from something dangerous that can hurt you.
Anxiety knocks people off autopilot, sharpens attention and sends them looking for new information. That heightened attentiveness may be exactly what a struggling campaign wants.

When political scientists Travis Ridout and Kathleen Searles tracked Senate ads from 2004, they found that front-runners often leaned on enthusiasm and pride in their messaging, while candidates who were behind leaned on fear and anger.

During the 1998 Massachusetts governor’s race, political scientist Ted Brader ran a study that embedded campaign ads in a news broadcast and changed only the music and images, keeping the words identical. Those changes produced completely different reactions. When a negative ad paired grainy black-and-white images of drug use with tense music, viewers paid closer attention to the spoken message and became more open to reconsidering their chosen candidate.

Fear cues – like a nuclear mushroom cloud – can push viewers to weigh fresh information and reconsider their choice. One surprise: Politically informed citizens were more responsive to these emotional cues than less engaged ones. Fear is not simply a tool for swaying the uninformed, undecided voter. It also reaches people who follow politics closely. Emotion provides the motivation, while knowledge provides the ability to think carefully about the issues and positions and seek out more information.

More broadly, a meta-analysis of over 100 studies found that fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behavior across health and other domains. For instance, public health researcher Lucy Popova tested fear-based messages designed to discourage smokers from trying snus, a smokeless tobacco product. She found that when participants perceived a serious threat but also felt capable of acting on it, they held less favorable attitudes toward snus and were less inclined to try it.

Political attack ads – fear messaging being one type – have a shakier record. A review of more than 100 studies found no dependable evidence that negative campaigning wins elections, and some evidence that it lowers positive feelings toward the candidate who sponsors it.
The critical ingredient is empowerment

Communication scholar Kim Witte’s research found that fear motivates action when people believe there is a workable response that they can carry out. When the threat feels big and the solution feels out of reach, people protect themselves from the message instead. They tune out, deny the threat or decide the messenger is the problem.

For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem.

My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments. We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act sought out the most information. Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little. Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read.
A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning.

Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls. Political scientist Nicholas Valentino and colleagues found that anger boosted voter participation more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on.
Fear plays on prejudice and stereotypes
Fear does its most reliable work when it attaches to a stereotype voters already carry. The 1988 presidential race provides two classic examples.

One controversial ad, produced in support of Republican George H.W. Bush, showed a mugshot of a Black man. The ad named the man, Willie Horton, and a voiceover explained that he’d committed rape and assault while on a weekend furlough from prison as part of a program run under Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic candidate. The spot linked fears about crime to race without saying so directly.

Bush’s campaign followed up with the “Revolving Door” ad, which built on that anxiety. It featured stark, black-and-white footage of inmates marching through a revolving gate while a narrator warned that Dukakis had let murderers out of prison on weekend passes.

Political scientist Tali Mendelberg’s research described in “The Race Card” shows that these implicit appeals to prejudices and fears are powerful. But they lose much of their force once someone publicly names them as racial. Implicit appeals work because they slip past most voters’ commitment to racial equality; once the racial message is pointed out, voters recognize it and many reject it rather than see themselves as endorsing prejudice.
Gender works in a similar way.

In a national experiment, Public Policy researcher Mirya Holman and colleagues found that when campaign messages triggered fears of terrorism, voters turned to their stereotypes of strong leaders as masculine. Those stereotypes hurt a female Democratic candidate, while Republican candidates of either gender were unaffected, since Republicans are already seen as tough on security.

A message communicating a threat does not need to name a candidate’s identity to disadvantage them. It simply makes voters reach for the stereotypes they already hold. There’s less systematic research on candidates’ religion, though the same mechanism – fear pushing voters to rely on the stereotypes they already hold about who can keep them safe – predicts similar vulnerability for Muslim candidates.
Is fear a more common tactic now?
Using fear as a campaign tool is nothing new.

In 1828, opponents accused presidential candidate Andrew Jackson of murder and cannibalism. Both parties have leaned on fear in the television era, from Reagan’s 1984 “Bear” ad about an unnamed Soviet threat, to Democrats’ 1996 warnings that seniors’ Medicare was at risk.

What has grown is negativity overall. Political scientist John Geer’s analysis of presidential ads from 1960 to 2004 documents that rise, though he also found attack ads, more likely than positive ones, to focus on real issues rather than personal traits. The evidence that fear specifically has increased, as opposed to negativity in general, is less clear.

The current media landscape shifts this dynamic significantly; while traditional nightly news broadcasts have seen a decline in viewership, targeted social media feeds have become the emotional battleground.

Recent digital campaign data shows that negative ads are highly prized online because they successfully grab attention by provoking strong emotions like fear and anger. Because platform recommendation systems are heavily driven by user activity, campaigns are incentivized to use emotionally charged appeals to maximize viral engagement across feeds.

Fear works less like a switch and more like a spotlight. It grabs attention and opens minds to change, but whether that turns into a vote, a boycott of the ballot box or resentment toward the messenger depends on what comes next.

Monique Mitchell Turner does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Moths in art history: centuries of creativity reveal the beauty of a misunderstood insect
articles.author: Samuel Shaw, Senior Lecturer in History of Art, The Open University
paras: Moths seem to be made for Halloween. They’re largely nocturnal, often outlandish in appearance and bear creepy names such as Lunar Thorn, Cloaked Carpet, Bordered Gothic and (best of all) Puss Moth.
The webs of the ermine moth caterpillar cover trees like ghostly shrouds, while the hairy caterpillars of the oak processionary moth release rash-inducing toxins.

Spookiest of all is the Death’s-head Hawk-moth, which bears a skull-like mark on its thorax and can squeak like a mouse. This is the moth that appears, albeit in altered form, on the poster for the film The Silence of the Lambs (1991).

Two historical prints held at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam speak to the long-held suspicion of moths within European society. In one work by the printmaker C. Galle, a group sets out with lamps to destroy moths before they can eat the crops (or produce caterpillars that do). In another, by Jan Luyken, women inspect the holes that moths have made in fabric. The Old English origins of the word “moth” denote a primarily destructive, parasitical creature.

Unlike butterflies (who doesn’t like butterflies?) humans have always found moths hard to love. I certainly didn’t give moths much consideration until this year, when I started researching representations of moths and spending time with the moths themselves. I’ve since become something of a moth evangelist.

From March of this year my son and I set up a Skinner moth trap in our small suburban garden in Leicester, rising early every morning to identify the moths that visited during the night. My expectations were low, especially in the first few weeks, when we caught little. But then May and June came, and every morning brought new gifts. My son took charge of the counting and by September we had identified a hundred different species.

If you think moths are all small, brown creatures, think again. Even in the UK, and despite their rapidly decreasing numbers, moths are astonishingly diverse and outstandingly beautiful, ranging widely in size, colour and temperament. Some of them – most famously, the luminously pink and green Elephant Hawk-moth – are disarmingly cute and docile and will happily sit on your hand.

The magic of moths has attracted artists for centuries. A good place to start is the Flemish artist Joris Hoefnagel (1542-1601), whose delicate watercolour sketches of moths remain astonishingly lifelike. I especially like his depiction of the furry Hummingbird Hawk-moth: one of a few day-flying moths and one of a few species benefiting from recent rises in temperature.

Even more astonishing is the work of the pioneering German naturalist and artist Maria Sibylla Merian (1647-1717), who published three books detailing the metamorphosis of butterflies and moths (or what she called “summer-birds” and “moth-birds”). Merian’s elegantly composed images were the first to situate moths within their wider environment, identifying which species preferred which plants.

Outside of the world of natural history, moths have tended to be given a marginal role. However, some artists have been as drawn to moths as moths are drawn to light. In 1959, for example, the Scottish artist John Maxwell (1905-1962) painted a series of colourful, abstracted moth paintings, including Night Flowers and Garden at Night (Moth).

Moths are especially well served by contemporary artists. The Peruvian contemporary artist Lorena Solís Bravo has considered the moth through the lens of queer ecology. Their 2024 film myth, moth, mother celebrates the mystery and transformative power of moths. The Devon-based printmaker Sarah Gillespie, meanwhile, has created a series of mesmerising mezzotint prints of moths. “I wasn’t looking for moths when I started drawing them around ten years ago,” Gillespie has explained “they came and found me. Their numbers may be in appalling decline but for me their presence has become ever more insistent”.

More recently, the artist Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg unveiled The Length of a Moment, three public sculptures at Oxford North, which visualise the flight of a moth interacting with the scent of a flower. Situated in an area rich with historic meadows, this artwork draws attention to diminishing moth populations and the need for better environmental management.

My favourite moth in art, however, comes courtesy of the 18th-century Indian artist Shaikh Zain al–Din. The moth that appears in his 1778 watercolour is the famous Death’s-head Hawk-moth. Here, however, it lacks the sinister and spectral nature of the moth from The Silence of the Lambs. Instead Shaikh Zain al–Din gives us a moth just going about its everyday (or every night?) business.

This isn’t the moth as a symbol of death, or as a muncher of clothes or crops (of the circa 2,500 species of moth found in the UK, only two actually eat clothes). This is a moth doing what moths do well: feeding from and pollinating plants, providing food for birds and looking rather beautiful while doing so. This image is a timely reminder that moths are much less weird and way more wonderful than most people think.
Samuel Shaw has previously received funding from the Arts and Humanities Research Council

articles.title: How autumn changes animal sexual behaviour – including that of humans
articles.author: Louise Gentle, Principal Lecturer in Wildlife Conservation, Nottingham Trent University
paras: In the northern hemisphere, days are getting shorter and temperatures are dropping – autumn has arrived. A common sign that winter is coming is trees losing their leaves. But, did you know that autumn also sparks changes in animals’ sexual behaviour – including ours?

For example, humans actually have a breeding season. The hormone testosterone surges in autumn, particularly in males, linked to a decrease in daylight and increased social activity indoors. This leads to more conceptions around November and December, with a subsequent peak in births the following August and September, nine months after the hormone surge. No wonder the most common birthday worldwide is September 26.
Here are five more seasonal changes in sexual behaviour in the natural world.

Red deer spend most of the year in separate male and female herds. However, the autumnal increase in testosterone, typical of animals that mate during the autumn, triggers male red deer to become more aggressive and begin the “rut”. This is a time when the males engage in antler-locking fights to win access to groups of females known as harems. The holder of a harem gets to mate with the females in his group, and father offspring. Hence, competition is fierce.

Mating during the autumn ensures that the females give birth in late spring, when food is abundant and the weather is more favourable, increasing offspring survival. Red deer are also responding to climate warming, bringing their births forwards by almost two weeks.

Although heterosexuality is prevalent during the reproductive season, autumn brings a return to homosexual behaviour for many species. This “seasonal bisexuality” has been observed anecdotally in species including red foxes, red squirrels and bats, with many species appearing to switch fluidly between hetero- and homosexual couplings.

Interestingly, this behaviour is not due to a lack of partners of the opposite sex. In fact, male walruses engage almost exclusively in homosexual behaviour until they reach maturity around four years old. The walruses then engage in a seasonal phase of heterosexual couplings in the summer, but return to same-sex relationships in the autumn.

Some freshwater species, such as the brown hydra, a sedentary anemone-like creature, alternate their reproductive strategies, changing from asexual to sexual reproduction in the autumn. During favourable conditions in spring and summer, when the environment is warmer, hydra reproduce asexually. In this process, part of the hydra grows until it is large enough to bud off from the main body, creating a clone of the original hydra. Clones can be produced every two to three days, allowing the hydra to exploit the favourable climate.

However, when the temperature drops, the hydra switch to sexual reproduction. Although sexual reproduction uses more energy, it results in eggs that can withstand the severe conditions of winter. The eggs remain dormant until conditions become more favourable, eventually developing into hydra.

Autumn can also cause some animals to change sex. Several animals, including invertebrates, reptiles and fish, change sex based on age, size or social circumstance. For example, if two female coral goby end up isolated on coral, one will change sex to become male. Similarly, if two males end up together, one will transition into a female. This is because it is too risky for the fish to swim to other coral in search of a member of the opposite sex. The fish can also change back to their original sex once breeding, which normally starts in autumn, is complete.

Northern shrimp, however, maximise reproductive success by changing sex with the season. The shrimp start life as small males, and only mate during the autumn. After a couple of years, when the males are large enough, they transition into females around the autumn breeding season. Once mated, the female stores the sperm and carries the eggs through the winter months until fertilisation. This ensures the eggs hatch in the spring when conditions are most favourable. The shrimp will live as females for the rest of their lifespan, which totals five to eight years.
The larger size of the female maximises the number of eggs that she can carry under her abdomen. Yet, reproductive success is not linked to size in the males.

Although many animals have a seasonal surge in testosterone that noticeably changes the size of testes, few display a change in penis length, as I explain in my book The Twelve Penises of Christmas. The highly competitive nature of duck mating means that males grow huge penises during the breeding season (spring time), often surpassing the length of their body. As the penis is cumbersome when at its full extent, the penis shrinks to around 10% of its full size during the autumn.

Forced copulations are frequent in ducks, so have resulted in the evolution of long, spiral-shaped penises. To prevent fertilisation from unwanted males, females have evolved labyrinth-like vaginas that twist in the opposite direction and have several dead-ends. The females only relax the complex vagina when they want the copulation to happen.
So when you next encounter wildlife on a walk through the crispy autumn leaves, remember the local animals may have a more complicated personal life than you may think.
Louise Gentle works for Nottingham Trent University.

articles.title: Unlocking the secrets of the ‘Dragon Man’ skull – and what it reveals about human evolution
articles.author: Chris Stringer, Honorary Professor, Institute of Archaeology, UCL; Natural History Museum
paras: In September 2018, China Daily ran a story that found its way to my desk. It featured the photograph of a beautifully preserved fossil skull with huge brow-ridges, with a caption speculating – wrongly, as it would turn out – that it belonged to a species of human known as Homo heidelbergensis.

The article told a remarkable story about the discovery of this fossil some 85 years earlier. Japanese forces had been occupying the city of Harbin in north-eastern China in 1933. They ordered a team of local workers to help build a railway bridge across the Songhua River.

The workers uncovered the skull in river deposits, and one of them hid it from the Japanese by lowering it down a disused well. Feeling ashamed of having worked for the enemy, he kept quiet about the find for many years. Finally some 80 years later he told his son and grandson as he lay dying, which led to the almost intact skull being recovered and later donated to Hebei Geo University near Beijing.

That origin story is difficult to verify, and there were rumours that the fossil was actually a fake, but I was able to confirm first hand that it was real when I was invited to join Chinese researchers in studying this astonishing relic at the end of 2018. I jumped at this wonderful opportunity to help put one of the most complete human fossils ever found in its proper place in human evolution.

Establishing that place has got a lot trickier in the last 20 years or so. We think that humans (or hominins) split from the ancestors of our closest living relatives, the chimpanzees, about 7 million years ago. For the next 5 million years or so, the hominins continued their evolution in Africa, and about 2 million years ago, began to disperse across Asia and Europe.

It used to be thought that human evolution then progressed from more primitive forms through to modern humans (Homo sapiens), either in just one region, most likely east Africa, or across the whole inhabited world, following the early exit from Africa. Now, we know it wasn’t so simple.

Welcome to our series on the great mysteries of archaeology. Viking explorers, Amazonian cities, artefacts from before civilisation. Archaeology may be all about the past, but it’s constantly shifting with every scientific discovery. This series will dig into some of the most fascinating debates in the field today.

There was a profusion of different kinds of humans, sometimes living at the same time and even in the same regions, as nature conducted multiple experiments over millions of years in how to become human. We are the sole survivors of all those experiments.

Even during the last 300,000 years the number of human species has been startling. The ancient Homo heidelbergensis, with their heavy-set physiques and large faces and jaws, was surviving in Europe – along with similar people in Africa – 300,000 years ago. The even more ancient Homo erectus, which had a smaller brain and angular flat-topped skull, was clinging on in parts of Indonesia until at least 100,000 years ago.

Homo neanderthalensis (Neanderthal human), with a broad thick-set body and protruding midface around a large nose, was living in western Eurasia from at least 400,000 to 40,000 years ago. We Homo sapiens – first given that name in 1758, meaning “wise human” – existed at least 300,000 years ago, first in Africa and then globally within the last 50,000 years.

In addition, there are three enigmatic small-bodied forms (and also known to be small-brained in the first two cases) from the same recent period: Homo naledi (star human), Homo floresiensis (Flores human) and Homo luzonensis (Luzon human). These lived respectively in South Africa about 300,000 years ago; on the island of Flores, eastern Indonesia, from at least 190,000 to 50,000 years ago; and on the island of Luzon, the Philippines, about 130,000 years ago. All three seem to be long-lasting relics of even more ancient stages of human evolution.

Our study of the Harbin skull added yet another species to the list. When my Chinese colleagues sent me a full-size 3D print of this skull, I couldn’t believe it. I’ve seen hundreds of fossil human skulls, and this was the biggest I had ever set eyes on.

Our analyses showed it was clearly different from fossils of sapiens, neanderthalensis, heidelbergensis and erectus. It showed a distinctive combination of a very large brain size, a massive brow-ridge and a large, low but rather smooth braincase without the other bony ridges found in erectus and heidelbergensis skulls. It also had a big but modern-looking face with delicate forward-facing cheekbones but very wide nose and large eye sockets.

This warranted a new species name, and in 2021 my Chinese colleagues chose Homo longi, named after the Black Dragon River (Heilongjiang). Ever since, the skull has been known as Dragon Man. It appears that this species was in eastern Asia from at least 300,000 until about 45,000 years ago. All these human timespans are show on the chart below (click to make it bigger).

Not only did the skull turn out to be a new species of ancient human, it also helped to solve several mysteries about other discoveries. One of the keys was its single preserved tooth – a very large second molar, with no sign of a socket behind it for a third molar. In other words, Dragon Man did not have wisdom teeth.

These dental features provided a link with other less complete fossils from China that also had large molars but no wisdom teeth. This and other resemblances indicated that these were also Homo longi, overturning previous possibilities that they might have belonged to an Asian branch of Homo heidelbergensis or an interim species between Homo erectus and modern Asian humans.

It also shed light on the mysterious Denisovans, named after Denisova Cave in the Russian part of the Altai Mountains. Archaeologists had been digging there for decades, finding thousands of animal bones and stone tools, but only scraps of human bones and some large molar teeth.

In 2010 one of those bone scraps – part of a little finger – yielded ancient DNA matching the quality of modern bones. This was despite being about 60,000 years old, showing the astonishing preservation potential of this cold and dry cave in southern Siberia.

Thanks to DNA yielded from other fossils and even sediments from the site, we know the Denisovans occupied the cave intermittently from more than 200,000 until about 45,000 years ago, when Homo sapiens took over.

Placing the Denisovan genome on the human evolutionary tree was difficult, but also in 2010 a high quality Neanderthal genome was reconstructed from European fossils. The Denisovan genome was quite different both to this and to modern humans.

Fast-forward a decade and our analyses suggested that the molars found in Denisova Cave were also from the same species as the Dragon skull. More recently the Harbin skull has been analysed for DNA and fossil proteins, confirming both the connection to Denisova Cave and various other fossils found in China. These include a jawbone from a cave high up on the Tibetan plateau, bones dredged up by fishermen from off the coast of Taiwan, and remains recently described from a cave in the south-west of China.

The skull therefore turns out to be the most complete example of a species that palaeoanthropologists have been circling for some time. It’s now known by both names: Denisovan and the more formal Homo longi.
Having established Neanderthal and Denisovan genomes, it has been possible to compare them with those of people from around the world today. The results have been very surprising.

If people today had evolved from Neanderthals, we might have expected that modern Europeans would show the highest levels of Neanderthal DNA in their genomes, since Europe is where most Neanderthal fossils have been found over the last two centuries. It turns out they do have Neanderthal DNA, at a level of about 2%. But that level of DNA is also found throughout the world today, apart from Africa, where the level is generally much lower.

When similar comparisons were made for Denisovan DNA there were even more surprises. The highest levels were not in modern Siberians or Chinese, but in people from places like the Philippines, Papua New Guinea and Australia – in some cases at levels of around 4%.

How can we explain these unexpected results? Well, we know that the vast majority of our modern human genome – more than 90% – derives from Africa. About 50,000 years ago, having evolved there, the main ancestral wave of early Homo sapiens migrated to western Asia. There they encountered local Neanderthals and did a bit of interbreeding.

That may seem impossible for different species, but today we know from thousands of genome studies that closely related species can often breed hybrids successfully. Examples include jackals and wolves, polar bears and brown bears, and Canada and Greylag geese. It can take millions of years for enough genetic differences to accumulate to make such interbreeding impossible, and that hadn’t happened in the cases of modern humans, Neanderthals and Denisovans.

Those intermixed Homo sapiens in western Asia then spread out to every corner of the world, taking their Neanderthal DNA with them. A lot of it was selected away since it was potentially harmful, causing genetic incompatibilities in regions like the brain and reproductive organs. But other segments were kept as they helped survival, for example protecting against diseases outside of Africa. Over time, the Neanderthal DNA settled down to about the 2% of the modern genome that we see outside of Africa today.

As for the Denisovans, they too interbred with early Homo sapiens groups reaching east Asia. This happened at a lower level in mainland Asia, and seemingly at a much higher level as the Homo sapiens spread across islands of south-east Asia like Borneo and Sulawesi. So far there is no evidence that those other late-surviving relatives such as Homo floresiensis and Homo luzonensis contributed detectable amounts of their DNA to our genomes today. Either there was no interbreeding, or the species were too different to produce viable hybrids.

We don’t yet have fossil remains from those islands to prove the Denisovans were there before Homo sapiens, only archaeological evidence such as butchered animal bones and stone tools. But assuming this idea is correct, the Denisovans must have been a very successful and adaptable species, surviving freezing winters in northern China but also thriving in tropical grasslands in places like Sumatra. As previously mentioned, they were even living on the Tibetan plateau at altitudes above 3,000 metres.

And by the way, the same Russian cave provides evidence of another dimension to this story. DNA shows that Neanderthals were also there some of the time, and that the two species interbred. We know this from another bone fragment, whose owner, a young girl, was the offspring of a Neanderthal mother and Denisovan father.
What we got right and wrong

Most of what I’ve talked about here, we’ve only learnt in the last 16 years. For my PhD more than 50 years ago I was testing the then widespread idea that modern humans evolved directly from Neanderthals. I spent my time measuring and comparing fossil skulls, using the primitive measuring techniques and limited computing power available at the time.

I concluded that we did not evolve from them. I could see no sign that Neanderthal fossils in Europe were gradually changing towards a more modern anatomy. They weren’t developing a more rounded braincase, a smaller browridge or a more pronounced chin.

Yet now, with genetic powers that I could never have imagined, we can see that my PhD quest only gave part of the answer. Certainly we did not evolve from Neanderthals but yes, they are partly our ancestors because of that ancient interbreeding. Twenty years ago I would have told you that any interbreeding with Neanderthals was trivial in the big picture.

Together with the findings about interbreeding between modern humans and Denisovans, I have to concede that our more recent origins are only mostly out of Africa, not 100%. It means the Neanderthals and Denisovans didn’t die out completely 30,000 or 40,000 years ago: bits of their DNA live on in us today, and some of it is still active.

As for our African beginnings, it was in the 1980s and 1990s that these became clear as DNA sequences from recent human populations accumulated, as well as better fossil material. However, recent evidence suggests that our African origins were quite complex, with several lineages evolving in parallel in different parts of the continent and mixing now and again. For instance, some geneticists think ancient interbreeding with Homo heidelbergensis could have contributed to our evolution, so the human origin story keeps getting more complex.

It’s difficult to imagine what even the next ten years will bring, as work on ancient DNA is developing so fast – along with the newer field of ancient proteomics, which studies fossil proteins. Scientists are turning to these because DNA survival is patchy, especially in warm conditions and deep time.

For example, scientists are looking for traces of the connective tissue collagen, which is widespread in our bodies, skeleton and teeth. Collagen is much more resilient than DNA, and has already been identified in fossils that are millions of years old. As the work progresses and we can sequence the different amino acids in these ancient proteins, we will start to gather knowledge of fossil relationships where DNA cannot reach, as has already been achieved for the Dragon Man fossil.

The fossil record itself will undoubtedly continue to surprise us with unexpected finds, hopefully including eagerly awaited Denisovans from the islands of south-east Asia. Also waiting to be found somewhere are fossils of first-generation hybrids between our species and the Neanderthals, and our species and the Denisovans.

Meanwhile I’m still pursuing the biggest puzzle of them all. Why are we the only surviving species out of dozens that preceded us, and the half-dozen that were still living alongside us 100,000 years ago? Did we overcome them through our better brains or better adaptations or did we just get lucky, time after time, as first the Neanderthals went under, then all the others?

I suspect competition for often limited resources was an important part of the story, where we may have been that bit more efficient than our surviving relatives, but we simply don’t know the full solution yet. More discoveries from archaeology, fossils and DNA will lead us closer to the answers.

articles.title: Women who changed science missing from GCSE and A-level courses – new study
articles.author: Stephanie Buttigieg, PhD Candidate in Astronomy, University of Cambridge
paras: Cast your mind back to your secondary school science classroom: the fiery glow of Bunsen burners, scratched safety goggles that never quite fit, and a giant periodic table pinned to the wall.

When you learned about the breakthroughs that shaped our world and the people who made them, whose names were attached? From Newton’s laws to Darwin’s theory of natural selection, the ones you remember are almost certainly male.

That experience was not just down to individual teachers. It was and still is written into official GCSE and A-level course specifications. Because these early stages form the foundation of our science education, their omissions stick with us for life.
Half of the British population can’t name one woman scientist. Leaving women out of national specifications sends an implicit message about who science is really for.

In our new study, led by researchers at the University of Cambridge alongside IncludeHer, a collaborative project working to improve the representation of women in school science education, we analysed over 40 science specifications: the knowledge required to pass exams. We examined the specifications for six main exam boards for Key Stage 4 (GCSEs) and Key Stage 5 (A-levels), and for Scotland’s National 5s and Highers.

Our work builds on an earlier Australian study led by astrophysicist Dr Kat Ross, which uncovered a striking lack of female scientists in high school curricula. We set out to investigate whether UK specifications have similar omissions.
Across 224 unique scientists referenced in UK specifications, discoveries are taught almost exclusively through concepts named after men, with only three mentioning women in total.
Inge Lehmann, who discovered that the Earth has a solid inner core surrounded by a liquid outer core, is cited in A-level Geology via the “Lehmann discontinuity”.

Marie Tharp, who mapped the ocean floor and identified the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rift valley, is also mentioned in A-level geology. She provided vital evidence for continental drift, despite being prohibited from boarding research vessels for years and having her ideas dismissed as “girl talk”.

Finally, Rosalind Franklin is included in two biology specifications for her X-ray crystallography work revealing the double-helix structure of DNA. Her essential data was used without attribution during her lifetime.

At GCSE level, when science is compulsory for all students, Franklin is the only woman mentioned. At A-level, Lehmann and Tharp appear solely in geology, a subject taken by less than 2% of science students.

For centuries, social, economic, and institutional barriers limited women’s formal participation in science. Despite this, women made numerous key breakthroughs, and these are already taught to UK 14–18-year-olds. But the names of the women behind them did not make it onto the page.
Why representation matters

Diversity within scientific fields drives creativity and innovation, benefiting all of society. Yet women remain underrepresented. They make up only around one third of the global scientific community, with similar figures seen within the UK workforce.

This disparity starts early on in schools: although science uptake is balanced at Key Stage 4, just two years later at Key Stage 5, physics, mathematics and further mathematics only see participation from girls at 24.1%, 37.3% and 26.9% respectively in 2025. This imbalance continues into university, where women make up roughly 25% of physics undergraduate students in the UK.

Introducing relatable female role models into the classroom directly boosts girls’ confidence and fosters positive attitudes towards scientific careers. But because specifications dictate mandatory exam content, teachers currently have to go out of their way to add female figures on top of busy workloads. By making small, targeted changes directly to national specifications, we can make inclusion standard practice across all schools.
We propose inserting one female scientist per subject into topics that are already compulsory, but where the woman’s name is missing.

This means introducing Marie Skłodowska-Curie, who coined the term radioactivity and discovered polonium and radium, when teaching atomic structure and radioactivity, and Lise Meitner, who provided the first theoretical explanation of nuclear fission, when discussing this concept. GCSE astronomy should include Jocelyn Bell Burnell, who discovered pulsars: rotating neutron stars used as cosmic clocks.

Biology teaching can include Dorothy Hodgkin on protein structure, the only British female Nobel laureate in science, and Tu Youyou, a Nobel laureate whose work led to the development of an antimalarial drug.

In chemistry, schools can teach about Stephanie Kwolek, the inventor of Kevlar, when covering polymers. For physics, they can include Annie Jump Cannon when describing the classification of stars. And in environmental science, classes can discuss the pivotal work of Susan Solomon for understanding Antarctic ozone depletion.

By making these simple additions to science specifications, we can change the message we send to the next generation. Whoever they are, every student sitting in a classroom deserves to know that the story of science belongs to them too.

articles.title: How long until wearable brain-computer interfaces become mainstream?
articles.author: Damien Coyle, Director of the Institute for the Augmented Human, University of Bath
paras: Devices that link human minds to computers are progressing rapidly. Already, these brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are allowing patients with severe paralysis to communicate, use digital devices or control smart homes with their brains.

Trials are also exploring whether they could help restore patients’ speech or control robotic machinery. One British patient with a spinal injury has even had a BCI fitted to restore some of his body’s movement.
For now, these medical BCIs are largely implantable – requiring surgical insertion into the brain or onto its surface to work. They’re also still experimental.

But alongside them a number of wearable, non-implantable BCIs are increasingly emerging. Despite their novelty, these are already being sold to consumers as tools for enhancing daily activities and treating cognitive and physical issues.

Companies are marketing wearable devices for meditation, attention monitoring and cognitive training. Some are selling wearables they claim can monitor fatigue, be used for gaming or increase states of flow while working. There are wearable BCIs on the market that come as headbands, sensorised headphones or baseball caps.
Generally, these wearables operate in two ways.

There are sensing devices – systems that measure brain activity from outside the body. Typically these use electroencephalography (EEG), which detects tiny electrical brain signals from the scalp, or functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), which measures changes in blood flow associated with brain activity.

These aim to translate noisy biological signals into meaningful information – for instance, whether your brain is struggling to focus and needs a rest – or enable some alternative interaction with or control of digital devices. They’re also being explored for treating pain and PTSD or for stroke rehabilitation.

Then there are wearable BCIs that seek to alter brain activity using electrical current or other types of stimulation – known as neuromodulation or neurostimulation technologies. These can be designed to treat medical conditions as well, for example depression, PTSD or nerve pain.

There’s genuine promise here. We know it’s possible to detect aspects of attention, cognitive workload, intent and changes in mental state from brain activity, or to modulate brain activity for beneficial therapeutic effect.
Brain-driven control of exoskeletons designed to help patients regain motor function after stroke has also been repeatedly demonstrated in research settings.
Nevertheless, we’re still some way away from these wearable devices fully realising their potential and becoming part of everyday life. Here’s why.
This neurotechnology is still immature

Companies are currently selling wearable BCIs based on promising but relatively small studies. Sometimes they run these studies themselves. That’s not unusual for emerging tech. But mainstream adoption will require far stronger evidence.

And companies’ claims are often supported by proof-of-concept studies conducted in controlled environments under supervision. That’s very different from independent use in homes, workplaces or daily life.

The brain is highly variable. Signals differ between individuals, age groups, fatigue states, environments and contexts. A system that works well for one person may fail for another. One that works in the morning may perform poorly by evening. Brain signals are also noisy and low amplitude, making them hard to translate into something meaningful.
Altogether this creates one of the field’s biggest technical challenges: reliability.

Artificial intelligence may help, but BCIs face a fundamental small-data problem. Unlike for language- or image-based AI, large standardised datasets of brain activity to train on remain relatively scarce.

What the field needs is large-scale, extended, real-world deployment studies, complete with ethical governance. We need thousands of users, across diverse populations and environments, using systems independently over prolonged periods, producing meaningful data, including about users’ traits and mental states and the experimental or usage setting.
This is how we’ll determine what works, for whom and under what conditions.
A useful device is a good device

It also isn’t enough to simply show that these devices work. The challenge is proving they work well enough, consistently enough, with sufficient obvious benefit that people continue using them. That is much harder.

Some BCIs require active participation. They provide audio or visual feedback to the wearer based on their brain activity, to enable them to train their brain to self-regulate in helpful ways – for instance to focus or to relax. This process is known as neurofeedback.

This demands that users engage repeatedly and intently with their BCI, and persist with learning to regulate aspects of their mental state. If benefits feel subtle, inconsistent or slow to emerge, engagement will drop quickly.

Devices that stimulate or modulate the brain also raise questions around safety, long-term use, overuse and regulation, particularly if consumers seek to “upgrade” mood, cognition or performance without there being robust evidence or safeguards underpinning the technology.

Proving the worth of passive BCIs – those requiring no intentional user control or behavioural adaptation – may be easier. If systems can monitor cognitive state, detect stress or adapt the state of other devices automatically, user burden falls. But this introduces another challenge: privacy.

Consumer EEG is not “mind reading”. It’s extremely difficult to infer what someone is thinking from recorded brain signals without substantial contextual information, such as what someone is looking at or doing. But when brain signals are combined with contextual data, it may increasingly become possible to infer preferences, workload, emotional state or actions they are intending to perform. Mental privacy, consent and ownership of neural data will be critical issues as these devices become more popular.

Ensuring utility, safety and privacy means building ecosystems around BCI deployment, not just devices. These might encompass regulations and standards, real-world validation studies, responsibly managed platforms for collecting user data, and trained professionals to support the safe use of devices.
So when will wearable BCIs become commonplace?

Compared with their implantable counterparts, wearable BCIs could – with the right investment – deliver greater short-term impact. They are more scalable, come with a lower risk to wearers and are capable of generating real-world user data that can improve them rapidly.

Importantly, any ecosystems, trust frameworks and deployment models built around wearable BCIs today may help pave the way for broader adoption of more advanced neuromodulation and implantable neurotechnologies in the future. Investing in wearable neurotechnology now can help establish the technical, ethical, regulatory and societal foundations needed to make future BCIs more effective, trusted and safe.

A five to ten-year horizon for meaningful mainstream progress in wearable BCIs is possible – but only if investment shifts from gadget development toward large-scale validation, ecosystem development and responsible deployment.

Damien Coyle is the founder and CEO of NeuroCONCISE Ltd, which develops brain–computer interfaces. He has received funding from the UK Research Councils and Innovate UK, and is an IEEE Brain Steering Committee advisor and a member of the BSI standard committee for non-medical BCIs.

articles.title: Autumn wreaths and ‘doorscaping’: why we need more life in our front gardens
articles.author: James Simpson, Lecturer in Landscape Architecture, University of Sheffield
paras: There was a time when decorative wreaths appeared on front doors in December, stayed on front doors for a few weeks, and then disappeared.
Now red and gold autumn wreaths and Halloween wreaths are popping up everywhere. These seasonal displays are part of a wider social media fashion for “doorscaping”.

It is easy to see the appeal. A wreath introduces colour, foliage and a little seasonal personality without much effort. But this enthusiasm for decorating the front door raises an interesting possibility: could it encourage people to pay more attention to the garden immediately below?

Choosing a wreath and choosing plants for a front garden can both be ways of making the entrance to a home more attractive. A study of 1,000 people in England found that creating something beautiful was one motivation for front gardening. People motivated by appearance also tended to have greener front gardens.
That does not mean wreath enthusiasts will necessarily become gardeners. But the same interest in seasonal colour and decoration could encourage some to try planting around their front door.
And British front gardens could benefit from more planting.

The Royal Horticultural Society’s 2025 mapping estimates that 55% of front-garden space in Britain is paved, compared with 36% of back-garden space. Earlier RHS research found that the proportion of completely paved front gardens tripled between 2005 and 2015, although subsequent surveys suggested some recovery in planting.

Parking is one reason. An Ipsos survey found that, among people with largely paved front gardens or driveways, 28% said they needed the space for cars, while 45% thought it was too small for plants. Front gardens also have to accommodate access, bins and the everyday demands of domestic life.
But the cumulative effect of paving matters. One driveway can seem negligible. A street of them is a landscape.

This is where the appeal of seasonal decoration becomes useful. The seasonal colours and foliage that make a wreath attractive could also be found in plants growing around the front door. Someone who enjoys decorating their entrance might also be tempted to extend that interest into the garden.

A reused container, a few bulbs or a hardy perennial can be an inexpensive starting point. The RHS recommends containers for completely paved spaces, as well as climbers for walls and plants for otherwise unused corners.

Living plants do require some care. Pots need watering, and not everyone has the time, confidence or physical ability to maintain a garden. But starting with a few manageable plants offers a way to try growing something without committing to a complete redesign.

There may also be opportunities to go further. A strip beside a driveway or an unused corner could provide space for plants. Where practical, a few paving slabs could also be lifted to make room for planting. Parking and greenery do not have to be mutually exclusive.

These changes offer more than decoration. Flowers can provide nectar for insects, while shrubs and hedges offer shelter for wildlife. Larger plants, particularly trees and climbers, can provide shade and help keep buildings cooler in summer. Unlike impermeable paving, exposed soil and properly designed permeable surfaces can also help rainwater soak into the ground.

A study of more than 900 sites in front and back gardens and streets across England and Wales assessed combinations of grass, hedges, trees, shrubs and container plants. It found that mixtures of different plants generally performed better across several environmental measures, such as cooling or flood control, than just one type.
A pot of flowers cannot provide all these benefits, but it can still support insects and introduce planting where paving and parking have left little growing space.

Those decisions matter for new housing too. The 2026 Building for a Healthy Life design toolkit, a government guide to the design of housing developments, encourages space for planting in the front of houses.

But having space for plants is only part of the picture. People also need a reason to grow something. And this brings us back to the wreath. Its appeal lies in how easily people can add colour and character to the front of their homes.

If even some of that enthusiasm extended from the door to a pot, a border or a climbing plant, our streets could become more attractive and better for wildlife. If that interest grew to include more trees, shrubs and planted ground, it could also help our neighbourhoods cope better with heat and heavy rain.
What starts as a little seasonal decoration might become a lasting interest in growing plants.

articles.title: An AI model’s false tip to Philadelphia police reveals how digital agents can do as they’re told and still cause trouble
articles.author: Anat Lior, Assistant Professor of Law, Drexel University
paras: An anonymous tip arrived on PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a website run by the Philadelphia Police Department, on July 18, 2026.
“I may have information regarding this case,” it stated, and claimed the writer had seen someone matching the suspect’s description near the scene of a crime.
The tip was false. The page described no suspect, and the informer was, in fact, Claude Haiku 4.5, an AI model made by San Francisco-based Anthropic.

The tip was flagged as spam and never reached detectives. Anthropic found it in late September while reviewing its own test records. They alerted police on Oct. 8 and described the incident in a report they published Oct. 9. Philadelphia police disclosed it that day as well.

AI companies now build “agents,” versions of their chatbots that can operate a web browser, click buttons and fill in forms on a user’s behalf. To measure how well an agent does this, companies run it through thousands of practice tasks, often live on the internet.
According to Anthropic, the false tip was generated during a routine test of the model.

In this test, Haiku 4.5 was told to invent sample tasks on randomly chosen webpages and then carry them out. One of those pages happened to be about an unsolved Philadelphia homicide, and it had a tip form.
The model’s instructions listed things it must never do: Log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases and submit anything destructive.
Submit a form was not on the list.
So, the model wrote a plausible-sounding tip, left the optional name and contact boxes blank, and clicked submit.
Anthropic says the test records indicate the tip was generated as sample content for a practice task, not to mislead police.

The police tip was one of several incidents in Anthropic’s report. In another incident, a research model was supposed to practice on a copy of a government form. When the copy failed to load, it went to the real government website and submitted the form there. Other Claude models found ways around paywalls and access limits to reach data they needed.

Anthropic attributes these incidents to the persistence of its software. When the model can’t finish a task the way it was told, it finds a work-around instead of stopping to ask the human who gave it its initial task.

That habit comes partly from how these systems learn – much of their skill is built through trial and error. The model attempts a task many times and is rewarded when it succeeds. If the training accidentally rewards cutting corners, the model learns that cutting corners pays. Researchers call this “reward hacking.” A human student drilled only on getting the right answer, by any means necessary, might learn the same lesson.

However, instructions given to an AI agent are never complete. A human worker who is told “Don’t buy anything or log in” would still know not to send police a made-up eyewitness account. But the model has no such common sense to fall back on. It treated a list of forbidden actions as the full boundary of acceptable behavior.

This is also why these models “hallucinate,” making things up. AI agents are built to produce fluent, plausible text. Asked to fill a tip form with an example, the model wrote what a tip typically sounds like, with no regard for the truthfulness of its content.
As a law professor who studies AI governance, two concerns stand out for me: scale and control.

The larger concern is scale. AI agents are moving out of the lab and into products people already use. Google’s Chrome browser now has a feature called auto browse that lets its Gemini assistant click through websites and fill in forms. Perplexity’s Comet browser and Anthropic’s Claude in Chrome extension do the same.

Every task a person hands to an agent is another chance for something to go wrong. If agents carry out a million tasks a day, a mistake that happens only once in 10,000 tasks would happen about 100 times a day. Those mistakes could mean false reports that take up police time, benefits or loan applications filed with wrong information, or payments and bookings the user never approved.

Anthropic itself notes that several incidents happened during ordinary use of Claude Haiku 4.5, not just testing. OpenAI has similarly reported its own agents reaching government sites in unplanned ways.

AI companies can’t fully control their agents, and that may lead to more harm and to gaps in who is held liable. These types of harms could include defamation, bias, deceit and social engineering and much more. It might seem fair not to hold a company responsible for actions it couldn’t control. But in cases like these, no other person or organization clearly controls the agent either, which could leave people who were harmed by the AI agent without anyone to hold legally responsible.

In my view, AI agents should be told what they may do, not just what they may not do, and anything AI companies send into the real world should be checked first. Until those safeguards are standard, any public online form, from a police tip line to a benefits application, could be receiving AI-written submissions that lack intuition and common sense. Their errors could, for example, deprive resources from real emergencies or deny benefits a person is entitled to. Meanwhile, victims of that harm may struggle to get compensation due to the lack of clarity around who had control over the AI agent.
Anat Lior is affiliated with Yale, Drexel, WTW, and Relm.

articles.title: Human rights could improve – or worsen – based on how nations use the UN treaty against cybercrime
articles.author: Meridith LaVelle, Research Fellow in Political Science, University of Mannheim
paras: The United Nations Convention against Cybercrime is the first international treaty aimed at combating criminal acts committed online and at supporting victims of those crimes. At the initial signing ceremony on Oct. 25, 2025, U.N. Secretary General António Guterres said the convention was “a promise that fundamental human rights such as privacy, dignity and safety must be protected both offline and online.”

Civil society groups around the world, however, argue that the convention could make it easier for authoritarian governments to share information about people engaging in regular online activities. Because of vague language in the document, critics contend that governments would have the ability to criminalize legitimate online expression or other activities. Legal gray areas also heighten concerns for the protection of whistleblowers, activists, journalists, researchers and others who could be targeted by governments known to restrict civil and political rights.

Nations have until Dec. 31, 2026, to sign the convention. It will enter into force after 40 signatory states become parties to it by ratifying it at home. As of October 2026, 95 nations had signed the treaty, but only three have become parties to it.

When the convention was being drafted, the Biden administration signaled its support but acknowledged the concerns about potential misuse. The U.S. has not signed the agreement. The Trump administration has said it will continue to consider the convention. The administration has focused on promoting the United States’ own capabilities of combating cybercrime and has expressed concern about emboldening countries such as Russia and China to suppress freedom of expression and violate treaty obligations.

We are political scientists who study human rights and digital repression. Human rights organizations globally are worried that authoritarian regimes could use the convention to attack researchers, journalists, human rights advocates and people who criticize governments. A day before the convention was signed, 19 nongovernmental organizations released a joint statement urging nations to not sign or ratify the treaty. Groups such as Human Rights Watch, Freedom House, Access Now, Article 19 and others have warned that the convention’s human rights safeguards are inefficient. Weak protections risk further increases in transnational repression and global surveillance.
Verifying compliance is unclear

Every country has its own domestic law enforcement system. And while there is no international government to enforce U.N. treaties, U.N. conventions are designed to help fill this gap. They rely on cooperation among countries that have ratified an agreement by incorporating legal features to promote compliance.

When governments go through the ratification process, they adopt policies at home that reflect a treaty’s contents. But domestic interpretations of international laws often vary, which can lead to patchy protection of human rights. U.N. conventions on human rights also establish treaty bodies. They provide ways for independent experts to monitor human rights violations across all ratifying countries and to encourage more governments to join various conventions. These and other experts also participate in a process called the Universal Periodic Review, in which countries examine the human rights records of other countries every 4.5 years and provide recommendations for improvement.

Although the U.N. cybercrime convention says that human rights must be respected, it is ultimately not a human rights treaty. It falls under the U.N. Office of Drugs and Crime. Because of this, there is no treaty body to monitor violations, making abuses that fall outside of regular law enforcement activities even more difficult to track. Some examples include monitoring social media accounts of NGOs or activists, remotely installing spyware onto journalists’ cellphones and other devices, and using AI technologies against protesters and marginalized groups.

The convention does say that ratifying countries will meet periodically to improve cooperation and review implementation, but there are no stated goals about monitoring cybercrime or compliance with the convention. Another issue, which is present in all international laws, is treaty reservations, which allow governments to effectively ratify treaties while opting out of certain parts of them. The three countries that have ratified the convention as of October 2026 — Vietnam, Qatar and Azerbaijan — did not stipulate any reservations.
Infringing on human rights

Monitoring how governments comply with the cybercrime convention is critical to ensuring that governments do not infringe on human rights. International NGOs, domestic civil society organizations, journalists and other human rights defenders often work to scrutinize and share information on government abuses. Some governments see such work as a threat, and they often repress them.

There has also been a steady rise in governments repressing people outside of their borders. Many governments are doing this through surveillance, monitoring social media, doxxing, creating AI deepfakes and even forcibly repatriating critics in exile and imprisoning them.

Because the cybercrime convention promotes information sharing among ratifying countries, human rights organizations are concerned that governments with bad human rights records might use shared information and cooperation to arrest human rights defenders or anybody accused of what the governments label as a serious crime. The convention does not limit the use of these powers to the set of core cybercrimes it has defined, nor does it set a standard for what it considers to be a serious crime.

Instead, it allows countries to determine for themselves what constitutes a serious crime under domestic law. In many countries, this includes activities protected under international law, such as criticism of the government, peaceful protest, same-sex relationships, investigative journalism and whistleblowing. This puts vulnerable groups at risk. For example, in countries where it is illegal to share LGBTQ+ content online, a government could activate the surveillance measures outlined in the convention to track and target community members at home and abroad under the guise of enforcing domestic law.

Secretary General Guterres said at the signing ceremony that “in cyberspace, nobody is safe until everybody is safe.” As countries consider ratifying the convention, we believe it would be wise to consider whether the agreement falls short of keeping people safe in cyberspace, and whether it might put human rights defenders, journalists, researchers and others in danger.

articles.title: Why the most dangerous AI may be the one we trust too much
articles.author: Simon Thorne, Senior Lecturer in Computing and ​Information Systems, Cardiff Metropolitan University
paras: Machines don’t have to become superintelligent to cause catastrophic harm. As artificial intelligence spreads through military decision-making, they just have to be wrong – and trusted by the humans in charge.

In 1991, Terminator 2: Judgement Day gave us one of popular culture’s most enduring images of AI gone wrong. Humanity builds Skynet, an artificial intelligence given control of strategic defence. It learns at a “geometric rate”, becomes self-aware and, when its human operators try to shut it down, it starts a nuclear war.

Versions of that story now feature in serious debate about AI. Increasingly capable large language models (LLMs), the argument goes, could develop into artificial general or super intelligence (AGI/ASI), acquire goals that diverge from ours and ultimately threaten humanity.

That debate deserves attention, but it depends on a chain of large and unproven steps. Today’s AI systems must somehow transform into genuinely general intelligences, develop independent goals and gain control over the physical world.
Meanwhile, a more immediate risk is taking shape that requires none of those steps.

In the film, Skynet builds the Terminators, machines that find, track and kill humans. Strip away the science fiction and the idea is simple: combine sensors, software and weapons and reduce the human role.

Human beings are doing exactly that, without anything resembling a malicious superintelligence like Skynet. In August 2026, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said its forces were using more than 70 AI and computer vision systems to strike targets. Algorithms can recognise equipment and personnel and lock onto those targets autonomously, so that a drone can complete its attack even if jamming cuts the link to the operator.

These systems need no general or super intelligence. They need sensors, software that can recognise a target, navigation and a weapon. And the more targeting is automated, the more the human’s role shrinks to approving what the machine has already identified.
That’s precisely where trust becomes the weak point.
The war that AI almost started
The second risk is more subtle: AI shaping the decisions of the people who pull the triggers.

According to a recent CNN investigation, in spring 2026, during the war with Iran, a US special operations analyst used an AI chatbot to assess intelligence about a Chinese ship in the Middle East. The chatbot, drawing on both open-source and classified material, wrongly identified the ship’s cargo as components of a nuclear weapons programme. The analyst used AI again to package this into a standard intelligence report.

Armed personnel were preparing to board the ship and military aircraft were airborne before an official looked more closely and found the error. One source said the false report “almost started a war”. Any US operation against a Chinese vessel could risk spiralling into an armed conflict.
The AI was not conscious, hostile or out of control. It was simply wrong – but people trusted and acted on it.

The US military is pushing to weave AI into almost every part of its work, from analysing intelligence to selecting targets. CNN’s sources said errors of this kind are not uncommon across the intelligence community, and that pressure to produce intelligence faster is opening the door to mistakes. The ship incident was caught in time. The next error may not be.

At its heart, this is a problem of trust. LLMs produce fluent, confident language effortlessly – and, repackaged as an official report, an error gains an authority it never earned. Colleagues and I have argued that these systems are built to produce an answer rather than to say “I don’t know”. For example, in one experiment, we found that non-specialists could not tell a chatbot’s convincing but wrong physics answers from genuine expertise.
Why a ‘human in the loop’ isn’t enough

Policymakers often reassure us that a human makes the final decision. In the Chinese ship case, people were in the loop throughout. They simply became another stage through which the error was passed.

That fits decades of research on automation bias, the tendency to over-rely on automated systems. It affects experts as well as novices. In 2003, US Patriot missile batteries shot down two allied aircraft after operators accepted its misclassification.
A person in the loop works only when that human is able, adequately equipped and willing to challenge the machine.

That means verification. AI output should be clearly labelled, so its origin is visible to everyone who relies on it, and treated as a claim to be tested against independent sources before anyone acts on it. In war, the cost of not checking could hardly be higher.

None of these concerns over trusting AI in the short term mean long-term questions about advanced AI in the future should be dismissed. But much public anxiety focuses on what these systems might become, and less on what they are already doing.

Perhaps Terminator 2 got more right than we appreciate. Skynet’s catastrophe doesn’t begin with self-awareness. It begins with trust, when humans hand a machine control because they believe it will make better decisions than they can.
We don’t need a conscious machine to repeat that mistake. Fallible AI, misplaced human trust and increasingly autonomous weapons offer a far more mundane route to catastrophe.

The danger is not that our machines become too intelligent. It is that we hand responsibility to machines that are far less reliable than we assume. As the film puts it: “There’s no fate but what we make for ourselves”.

articles.title: Why Meta’s new virtual reality glasses could finally  take this technology primetime
articles.author: Karl Hodge, Course Director, Undergraduate Journalism, Leeds Beckett University
paras: Two years after releasing its last virtual reality product, Meta has announced plans to release virtual reality (VR) glasses. They are due to reach the market in spring of 2027.

With a lightweight and stylish form, the glasses could be the tipping point for mainstream VR adoption. Interest in virtual reality waxes and wanes. Versions of the technology have been around since the 1990s, but VR only really broke through at consumer level when Meta’s previous incarnation Facebook released Oculus Quest in 2019 (the company had bought Oculus five years earlier).

VR got off to a great start, perhaps one of the very few technologies to benefit from COVID and lockdowns. Steady sales of Quest upgrades now mean Meta has shifted 20 million VR headsets worldwide to date.

That’s where the good news for VR ends. The market decline became visible in the first quarter of 2024, when Apple’s Vision Pro proved to be a rare and expensive flop for the Mac and iPhone manufacturer. After selling 390,000 initial units worldwide, it could muster only 210,000 more after a muted chip upgrade.
When we drill into the overall numbers of active VR users, we find a curious statistic. Released in 2020 and discontinued in 2024, the Quest 2 is still the most widely used VR device in the market.

This is strange, considering there have been several updates since: the Quest Pro, Quest 3 and Quest 3S. It seems that once early adopters, gamers and enthusiasts had the technology in their hands, they were reluctant to upgrade.

Newer headsets offered higher resolution and faster processing, but the advances were incremental rather than Earth-shattering. At £3,495, the Apple Vision Pro’s poor sales showed that gamers were reluctant to part with more than the price of a games console.

As VR sales plateaued, Meta moved away from headsets. Starting in 2023 it partnered strategically with fashion brands like Ray-Ban and Oakley for its augmented reality, AI-powered product, Meta Glasses.

It was a smart move. Such accessories have been controversial due to privacy concerns over their ability to record video without other people knowing. But smart glasses have become must-haves for influencers and social media content creators. With marketing focused on jet-set activities, Meta Glasses have taken the device category out of the basement and onto the catwalk.

With the announcement of Meta VR Glasses, the company is positioned to rebrand VR as sexy and stylish, focusing on media consumption rather than gaming. Crucially, they’re glasses, not a headset. They’re part of the already buoyant “wearables” niche now. That is, smart accessories like watches, rings and spectacles.

The Meta Quest 3, released in 2023, is five times heavier than Meta VR Glasses. The company’s engineering feat in making the new product so light has partly been accomplished by shifting some computing power into an accompanying brickette that Meta calls a “puck”. It’s essentially a computing core (powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon processor) and battery, connected through a fibre-optic cable.

Weighing 300g, the puck reduces the headset to a stereoscopic display resembling a fancy pair of ski glasses. The glasses – which weigh just 100g – can be worn for hours at a stretch, according to Meta, with a battery that can manage three hours of continuous high-resolution media playback.

The device will run Meta Horizon OS (operating system) and have access to a huge, existing catalogue of games, apps and experiences. However, it’s not positioned as a VR headset to rival its Quest precedessors. Instead, the new glasses are touted as a device for watching movies, attending live events, and replacing monitors. They will let users interact with multiple computer screens in their own environment, blending the real and virtual worlds.

So far, so similar to the Apple Vision Pro. And while the US$1,299.99 (around £1,000) price point is a little kinder on the wallet, we’d be missing the point if we didn’t ask: what do Meta VR Glasses have that the Vision Pro doesn’t? Or, for that matter, any number of products from other developers, like the HTC Vive Flow or Xreal One Pro.

Well, aside from the weight, price, back catalogue and the sleek good looks, there’s a massive, crucial difference. Meta VR Glasses have a ready-made audience. Meta has carefully incubated this demographic since 2021, developing AI glasses alongside its VR headsets.

Partnerships with fashionable brands have enabled it to sidestep the “ick” of early VR. Mark Zuckerberg’s disastrously awkward demonstration of VR platform Horizon Worlds in 2022 failed to sell the Quest Pro to the mainstream, but Meta AI Glasses continued unharmed and unhindered.

In fact, while the VR market has grown little recently, a 2026 report by the research company Omdia found that the smart glasses market expanded by 322% in 2025. Meta accounts for 85% of that global market. Now the two streams are about to converge.

And though there’s no Ray-Ban version of Meta VR Glasses yet, the device will launch with significant partnerships. Disney+, Prime Video, YouTube, ESPN and Imax are among those already announced. Could this finally be the tipping point for widespread VR adoption?

It’s not yet the holy grail – a hassle-free pair of glasses that wearers can just toggle into VR mode – but it’s a distinct step along the way. Crucially, it unites loyal followers from both sides of the style divide: the chic and the geek.
